title: 'Straight to the pool room':  Film classic The Castle goes onstage
text:
To mark 30 years since The Castle first endeared itself to audiences, the classic Australian film is being launched as a stage production.

The film is responsible for oft-quoted lines such as "How's the serenity?" and "It's the vibe" — and it can only be hoped that the stage version will have the vibe of the much-loved feature.

The tale of the Kerrigan family and the battle to save their home from an airport expansion will premiere at Melbourne's Her Majesty's Theatre in March 2027.

The stage adaptation has been penned by Rob Sitch, Tom Gleisner, Santo Cilauro and Jane Kennedy of the Working Dog production company, the four who wrote the original film.

The friends have been wanting to turn it into a live stage show for decades, they said in a statement.

"We wrote this new, fully updated show in the same way that we wrote the film screenplay all those years ago — the four of us in a room trying to make each other laugh."

They promised the stage show would be not just a retelling, but a celebration of the Kerrigan family that includes a quarter of a century's worth of funny updates.

One can only wonder what Darryl Kerrigan and his family would make of the internet, mobile phones and the building of a third runway at Melbourne Airport.

"When the team at Working Dog first approached me about bringing The Castle to the stage, I knew we had to do this," producer Michael Cassel said.

" The film miraculously captures the specificities of Australian life and yet feels so universally true; family love, the challenges change presents, and the warmth and humour and dignity of ordinary people standing up for what matters. "

The production will be directed by Heartbreak High and Fangirls director Paige Rattray, with set and costume design by Jonathon Oxlade.

AAP

title: Harvey Norman, Latitude issued $55m penalty for misleading ad campaign
text:
Harvey Norman and Latitude Financial have been issued a combined penalty of $55 million by the Australian corporate regulator for an advertising campaign that misled customers into taking out a credit card when buying products.

The penalty is the largest issued by the Australian Securities and Investments Commission (ASIC) to a company for misleading conduct.

Harvey Norman will be required to pay $35 million of the total penalty, and the remaining $20 million was issued against Latitude Financial.

Customers were hit with extra fees despite the "interest-free" arrangement. (Supplied: ASIC)

The case against the two businesses related to newspaper, radio and television advertisements published and broadcast to millions of Australians between January 2020 and August 2021 that spruiked 60-month interest-free payments and no need for a customer deposit when buying high-ticket items.

The advertisements "masked that consumers were required to take out a credit card, such as the Latitude GO Mastercard, to purchase goods, and were liable to pay monthly account service fees and, up to 15 March 2021, also establishment fees", according to ASIC.

The regulator argued customers who signed up to a GO Mastercard between March 16 and August 11, 2021, bought a Harvey Norman product using the 60-month interest free payment method and paid it off during that time, were liable to pay a minimum of $537 in additional fees.

Latitude Financial has been ordered to pay a penalty of $20 million. (ABC News: John Gunn)

Sarah Court, the regulator's chair, described the penalties as "a strong warning to the market" that reinforced "integrity in consumer marketing".

"Consumers were entitled to know that this offer involved more than simply paying for their purchase in 60 instalments," Ms Court said in a statement on Tuesday.

"The advertising encouraged consumers into an ongoing credit arrangement that carried additional costs and obligations.

" Today's outcome sends a strong message that businesses must give consumers a clear and accurate picture of the products they are promoting and the costs that come with them. "

Harvey Norman issued an apology to its customers after the ASIC ruling was released.

"While the Company did not intend to engage in false, misleading or deceptive conduct, the Company apologises unreservedly to the Court and customers," a statement said.

"The Company is committed to promoting a culture of compliance with all its legal obligations and will continue to work hard to comply with those obligations."

The retailer also posted an ASX update saying it had accrued at least $16.2 million "in anticipation of this possible outcome", but expected to record an additional financial hit this financial year due to the penalty.

Finance giant fined millions for spam Latitude Financial has been fined millions of dollars for a repeated breach of spam laws.

A spokesperson for Latitude told the ASX the company "accepts responsibility for its conduct and apologises to its customers".

The lender also said it "had "largely provisioned" funds to pay its $20 million penalty.

The penalties come after appeals lodged by legal representatives for Harvey Norman and Latitude Financial were dismissed in the Federal Court in September last year.

The businesses were first found in October, 2024 to have breached consumer law by misleading customers during the advertising campaign.

In his ruling on Tuesday, Justice Michael O'Bryan explained Harvey Norman had been issued a higher penalty than Latitude because the retailer "exhibited a different level of contrition".

"Public statements made by Harvey Norman's Chairman show a disregard for the potential harm suffered by consumers from Harvey Norman's misleading conduct," he said.

"A higher penalty is warranted to deter repetition and to motivate Harvey Norman to improve its compliance processes."

Both companies were also ordered to immediately publish corrected advertising on their website home pages for 90 days.

In April, Latitude Financial was also ordered by the Australian Communications and Media Authority to pay $3.96 million for breaking spam laws more than 2.7 million times.

The regulator found Latitude had sent more than 2.3 million spam messages between March, 2024 and April, 2025 that failed to include company contact information as required by law.

Almost 345,000 of those messages were sent without a working unsubscribe function, ACMA said.

The financial lender was also ordered to pay an additional $1.5 million in fines for similar breaches in 2022.

title: Hotelier tells ICAC he made 'mistake' trusting Liberal figures
text:
A hotelier who helped fund a conservative Liberal Party faction has told the NSW corruption watchdog he made a "mistake" trusting key figures at the centre of the bombshell investigation.

Part of the Independent Commission Against Corruption's (ICAC) probe is examining whether Michael O'Hara, a prohibited donor, made political donations "in amounts that were not declared and exceeded applicable donation caps".

It is alleged he used a company called Paslibdan Pty Ltd to make the donations, disguised as consultancy payments, to help stack the Liberal Party with conservative members.

Mr O'Hara, the first key witness in the Operation Rosny inquiry, said he was "absolutely astounded" and "disgusted" by allegations aired at the commission involving members of the right-wing faction known as the NSW Reformers.

The NSW Reformers are a conservative Christian Liberal factional group associated with several key figures in the inquiry, including founder and former Liberal powerbroker Christian Ellis, and Jean-Claude Perrottet, the brother of former NSW premier Dominic Perrottet.

Dominic Perrottet, who referred the allegations to ICAC in 2022, is not accused of any wrongdoing.

'I thought they were good people'

Counsel Assisting the Commission Peggy Dwyer SC questioned Mr O'Hara about invoices and emails detailing his payments to companies linked to Mr Ellis and Mr Perrottet, which referred to "strategic wealth strategy investment advice".

The key figures in ICAC investigation Eight weeks of public hearings by the ICAC that could change the NSW Liberal Party forever begin on Monday.

Mr O'Hara maintained he believed the arrangement was intended to promote his conservative values within the Liberal Party.

"It's like running a hotel where I might sit at the top and know what's going on, but I never interfere in the day-to-day operation when you've got good people, good managers, they run it," Mr O'Hara said.

"I thought they were good people … I made a mistake in supporting them because they obviously went off the track."

The commission previously heard Mr O'Hara was a prohibited donor because he "built a hospitality empire and has shares in numerous venues around NSW".

"As such, he is associated with a corporation primarily involved in the liquor and/or gambling industries and is prohibited from being a political donor," Dr Dwyer said on Monday.

title: The sun has set on the British Empire, and yet this celebration remains
text:
"It's just a square."

That's the three-star review of Nelson Mandela Place in Glasgow by someone named Katie Nicholson on Google.

Katie isn't entirely wrong. A statue for the freedom fighter and former South African president is set to be unveiled in October, but for now there's not a whole lot to see at the spot, listed as a tourist attraction on Google Maps.

But the couple of street signs tacked to buildings on West George Street, not far from the city centre, sit as an elegant and understated middle finger to apartheid South Africa.

The South African consulate left this location for some reason. (ABC News: Che Chorley)

In 1986, while Mandela was still in prison on Robben Island, the Glasgow City Council changed the name of St George's Place to Nelson Mandela Place.

It meant that the South African consulate under the then-ruling National Party was forced not only to see the name of one of their chief antagonists as they entered the Stock Exchange building every day, but also send out correspondence bearing his name.

They opted to use a PO Box address before moving from the location in the early 90s.

After Mandela was released, he came to the city to thank the people for their solidarity in 1993.

Nelson Mandela thanked Glasgow in 1993, between being released from prison and becoming president of South Africa. (Getty Images: Chris Bacon/PA)

"While we were physically denied our freedom in the country of our birth, a city 6,000 miles away, and as renowned as Glasgow, refused to accept the legitimacy of the apartheid system, and declared us to be free."

That cry of freedom is as synonymous with the Scottish as it is with Mandela himself.

So, how does a celebration of this Commonwealth sit with a city and country that has always had a fraught relationship with oppressors generally and the English specifically?

ABE – Anyone but England

Andy Murray got to represent Scotland in the 2022 Battle of the Brits. (Getty Images: Mark Runnacles/Battle of the Brits)

Tennis great Andy Murray once perplexed some (read: Americans) less au fait with the unique rivalries within the UK when he was asked who he'd be supporting at the 2006 FIFA World Cup and replied: "Anyone but England."

Scotland isn't on its own in this regard.

In the Ashes last summer, Australia's injury-plagued men's Test team scored a triumphant professional 4-1 victory, but more Australian joy was derived from watching another epic capitulation of an England team that had declared itself the saviour of Test cricket, teaching us all how to entertain, if not actually win much of anything.

We cheered every humiliating faceplant and fumble at least as much as we celebrated the all-time world-class performances of Travis Head and Mitchell Starc.

The recently completed World Cup was another reminder of the collective glee shared by so many in watching England stumble.

The Sun has set on the British Empire, and yet this celebration remains. (ABC News: Che Chorley)

There's just something about the schadenfreude for Scots, Aussies and dozens of other nations in watching England lose.

Sure, you've got the Parthenon Sculptures and Rosetta Stone, but we've got Ellyse Perry and Steve Smith.

"There is this standard, reflexive idea of that they would prefer almost everybody to win other than England, as the most powerful part of the United Kingdom," Western Sydney University emeritus professor of culture and research David Rowe told ABC Sport.

"I think for some people it's serious, for some people it's just a bit of fun."

Loading Instagram content

There are jokes to be made, but also reflections on the very real subjugation that went on for centuries, and arguably only ended in 1997 when Hong Kong gained its independence.

This celebration of empire remains a peculiarity as calls grow to decolonise our language and our lives.

For a perfect example, the Parthenon Sculptures mentioned earlier are more famously known as the Elgin Marbles, named for the lord who nicked them from Greece and brought them back to Old Blighty at the start of the 19th century.

"I mean, the Commonwealth of Nations is, let's face it, anachronistic," Rowe said.

Flags that don't always get to fly wave prominently at the Commonwealth Games. (ABC News: Che Chorley)

"There are people who … don't know much about it or, if they schooled up on it, educated themselves about it, would realise that this is an anachronistic organisation based on an empire that no longer technically exists."

Although, many in the still-constituent Scotland would tell you the legacy, if not the actuality, of the empire remains in many ways.

"There are plenty of people in Scotland, including its leading Scottish National Party, who really would prefer to separate from the United Kingdom and who are mightily displeased by Brexit," said Rowe, a sports sociologist who consulted on the Glasgow Life team tasked with helping boost the city's standing on the global sporting stage.

"There are plenty of Scots who felt a greater affinity with the European Union than with England."

Strange, anomalous and anachronistic

A time machine is perhaps a fitting vehicle of entry of an event harking back to the past. (AAP: Andrew Milligan/PA Wire)

At the opening ceremony of the 2026 Commonwealth Games, King Charles III and Queen Camilla were warmly welcomed by the packed crowd at Glasgow's Hydro, perhaps surprisingly considering the same crowd's hearty refrains of Flower of Scotland barely an hour later.

The Scottish anthem retells Robert the Bruce's legendary victory over King Edward II of England at the Battle of Bannockburn in 1314.

The thrust of the rousing choon, and Scotland's identity more broadly, is about how this small but mighty land of hard folk repelled the crown time and again on the back of sheer grit and pride.

So ingrained in their identity is sticking it to the English that, instead of tearing down statues of old royals and dignitaries like the Duke of Wellington, they have simply given up on removing the traffic cones placed on his head.

The Games have never opened like this – maybe they always should The 2026 Commonwealth Games are like no other that came before them and the opening ceremony was similarly unique in a way that will make it hard to go back.

And yet, twice in the past 12 years, Glasgow has gone out of its way to host what is correctly dubbed the Friendly Games, welcoming dozens of nations whose primary unifying theme is that they were once conquered by the "bastards" from that anthem.

"It does strike me as something of an irony that it's not that very long ago that Scotland had a referendum to sever its ties with the United Kingdom and the British Crown, and now it's hosting a Commonwealth Games," Rowe said.

"I think it's having a bit of fun, all the kilts and all the Scottish culture, reminding people that Scotland has its own identity and has not just been subsumed by the United Kingdom."

The Commonwealth Games has the royal seal of approval. (Getty Images: Aaron Chown/WPA Pool)

If you need more evidence of the strange bedfellows in effect, Rowe said you need only look at the event's original name.

It was called the British Empire Games from 1930 to 1950, the British Empire and Commonwealth Games until for the next four editions, and the British Commonwealth Games until 1972.

"So even more coded British," Rowe told ABC Sport.

"And it's a strange body in some ways, if you consider that it is a monument to colonialism and imperialism. And yet the members, most of whom were formerly under the jurisdiction of the British crown, were colonised, have now voluntarily agreed to join an organisation which was formed out of that imperial arrangement."

It also provides those in the British Isles a chance to beat England while representing Scotland, Wales, Northern Ireland, Guernsey, Jersey or the Isle of Man.

Scottish knights of the British Empire Chris Hoy and Andy Murray have won a combined 13 Olympic medals for Great Britain.

Duncan Scott is Team GB's most decorated Olympic swimmer, Mark Cavendish has won a world championship and Olympic silver with the Union Jack next to his name, but both turned around to beat the English while flying the Scottish saltire and Isle of Man's triskelion during the Commonwealth Games.

Duncan Scott has won more Olympic medals than any other British swimmer. (Supplied: Commonwealth Sport)

So how does the home crowd feel watching their sporting heroes flying those flags?

"I think it means more to them to compete for Scotland," one Glasgow local, Peter, told ABC Sport.

"You can see it in their faces when they do better. It does mean a lot more to them to represent their home country."

There's perhaps a hint of personal projection in this fan's assessment, as summed up by his mate, Pat.

"I would hope that it does [mean more] for them, because it would for me," he said.

Duncan Scott with the 2014 and 2026 mascots, the latter sporting a traffic cone for a horn. (Getty Images: Jane Barlow/PA Images)

No amount of raucous crowd support or national pride is going to turn a 45-year-old bricklayer who's had a hot dog for breakfast into a 10-flat 100m runner. But at the tippy-top of sport, where the margins are at their finest, it's got to be worth a few hundredths of a second.

Angharad Evans swam for Team GB at the 2025 world championships in Singapore, missing the semifinals and finishing a brutal 18th overall in the 100m breaststroke as she went almost two seconds slower than her time at the national trials.

She carried those scars with her until she exorcised them with a spectacular victory at the Tollcross International Swimming Centre, winning her first international gold medal and thanking the crowd for getting her to the wall 0.12 of a second ahead of Aimee Canny.

Angharad Evans said the Tollcross crowd carried her for the final 10 metres. (Getty Images: Quinn Rooney)

"Scotland was there to witness that and that was a very, very special moment for me," she said.

"I thanked them because leading into competitions it's so easy for doubts and negative thoughts to play a part in my mindset leading up, and I walk out and they just really uplift me and give me the confidence I need and boost me up.

"They often talk about how proud they are of us bringing back gold medals and PBs, but I'm immensely proud to have the Tartan Army supporting me in the crowd.

"Wearing the blue and white, hearing the crowd, being part of Scotland just carries you to the end. I don't think I would have had the strength and the courage I did in the last 10 metres if I wasn't in the blue and white and didn't have that crowd behind me.

"They absolutely helped me get to the end and finish in first place. So it's a medal for me but it's also a medal for Scotland."

All that from an English-born 23-year-old who is still learning the words to that famous Scottish anthem.

title: Origin Energy believes 900,000 customers' data accessed in breach
text:
Origin Energy believes the information of approximately 900,000 current and former customers was accessed during a recent data security breach.

The energy provider confirmed it first became aware of a potential security threat in early July but initially did not believe it credible.

The company has urged customers to be vigilant to scams and said specialist identity and cyber support services were available to affected customers.

"We have now completed the initial phase of our review into Origin's customer data security incident," Origin chief executive Frank Calabria said in a statement.

" To our customers, I am sorry. We don't take for granted the trust customers place in Origin and our safeguarding of their information. "

UNSW cybersecurity expert Richard Buckland described 900,000 people as "a lot of human suffering", but said the situation could be much worse, given Origin has more than 4.7 million customers, as well as details of former and potential customers.

Professor Buckland noted that numbers of people reported to be affected often changes as incidents are investigated.

Customers whose information has been accessed will be contacted, Origin said, and customer support hours extended.

"We are working with cyber security and forensic specialists to ensure the incident is contained, and we've taken a number of steps to secure our system," Mr Calabria said, confirming Origin was working with government and other agencies, and continuing its review into the incident.

Threat investigated since early July

Origin said it had been reviewing a "potential security threat" since early July.

"We worked to confirm its credibility and potential impact; however, based on the information available, it was not assessed to be credible," the statement said.

"On 22 July, new information emerged that indicated a potential security incident may have occurred.

"We acted immediately, providing updates to the market and notifying our customers as a precaution."

Professor Buckland described the situation as "quite strange".

" It is surprising. What extra information would have been needed to take the threat from non-credible to credible? "

He said many companies have proactive "bug bounty" programs, that offer a dedicated path for people to report cyber vulnerabilities so they can be fixed proactively.

There is little information available about the source of the breach, but whether the incident ends up having originated from outside or inside Origin, Professor Buckland said he would classify it as a cyber attack.

"These days, attackers just take the easiest path. Insider threats are actually quite serious to businesses and we’ve seen a growing number of these"

Alleged hacker went to media

On Wednesday last week, The Australian news outlet first reported an alleged hacker had sent it a sample of 50 customer records containing names, addresses, emails, dates of birth, phone numbers and bill history.

Origin Energy confirms hack Energy company Origin has confirmed that there has been unauthorised access and disclosure of some customers' data, a day after it announced it was investigating a "potential" breach.

The ABC later spoke to someone claiming to be behind the hack, who provided what they said was sample of data taken from a bigger customer list and internal screenshots of Origin computer systems.

The ABC has not been able to confirm with Origin that this data is legitimate.

Analysis of the sample showed it includes the real contact information that had not been publicly released in other major security breaches.

On Tuesday, Mr Calabria said it was a "criminal matter" that was now being investigated by the relevant authorities.

"Given this, we are constrained by the level of information we can provide about the incident at this time," the chief executive said.

Shares in Origin Energy were down more than 1.1 per cent by 12:30pm AEST on Tuesday.

title: Who is Ben Carroll, Victoria's 50th premier?
text:
Only a short drive from Darryl Kerrigan's fictional home in the classic comedy film The Castle, Airport West has shaped the political story of Victoria's new premier.

Live updates: Ben Carroll has become Victoria's 50th premier after Jacinta Allan stepped down from the state's top job

Ben Carroll's parents built their family home in the north-western Melbourne suburb back in 1974, a year before he was born — and two years before his future electorate of Niddrie was created.

The 51-year-old former lawyer and political adviser has now been sworn in as the state's next premier, taking leadership of the Victorian Labor Party after a chaotic party meeting set off by Jacinta Allan's resignation.

Jacinta Allan and Ben Carroll when they became premier and deputy premier respectively following Daniel Andrews's resignation in September 2023 . (AAP: Joel Carrett)

Like the members of the cinematic Kerrigan clan, Carroll has previously spoken about how his parents established a proud family business under the Essendon Airport flight path.

"In addition to building their family home, Mum and Dad also started their own small business, G B K Electrics — the initials stand for Greg, Ben and Kay," Carroll said in his inaugural speech in parliament after being elected the Member for Niddrie in 2012.

"Raising a family and establishing a small business at the same time is hard work. Mum and Dad succeeded at both.

" When I was growing up, dinner time was characterised by Dad putting the telephone off the hook so the family could sit down and have a meal together without interruption. "

A 36-year-old Ben Carroll won pre-selection to run in the 2012 Niddrie by-election. (ABC News)

When The Castle first hit cinemas in 1997, a young Carroll was studying law at La Trobe University and working part-time as a check-out operator.

"I spent eight years at Kmart in Airport West, which greatly assisted me during my college and university years," he said in that first speech.

"At this time, I also joined the union covering the retail sector — that is, the Shop, Distributive and Allied Employees' Association — and got a good understanding of the importance of unions in helping working people."

His union experience inspired him to become a political adviser under Steve Bracks, Victoria's Labor premier from 1999 to 2007.

Both Bracks and his successor, John Brumby, (who was premier from 2007 to 2010) have offered effusive praise of their former staffer.

Author and speechwriter Joel Deane said Carroll's leadership approach was likely to be more inspired by the Bracks–Brumby era, rather than a simple continuation of the Andrews–Allan years.

Deane wrote Catch and Kill about Labor's "golden four" of the 2000s — Bracks, Brumby, John Thwaites and Rob Hulls — and how they steered Victoria in a centre-left direction from the 1990s Kennett revolution.

"In some ways, Ben Carroll could be a throwback to the Bracks–Brumby era — socially progressive and fiscally conservative — but you never truly know until someone becomes leader," he said.

"You see some in politics, Labor and Liberal, and you don't know exactly what they stand for and wonder if it's just a career path.

"That's not the case with Ben. He's shown both a clear vision balanced with a pragmatic approach to progressive politics."

Former Victorian premier John Brumby on the day he was elected Labor leader to replace Steve Bracks in 2007. (Julian Smith: AAP)

Deane said Carroll's outlook has also been shaped by his work for federal MPs Bill Shorten and Stephen Conroy.

"Dan Andrews was a somewhat impulsive politician, always on the front foot and that certainly worked for many years. Bracks was inspired by Bob Hawke and in turn, Ben has been inspired by Bracks: a first-among-equals, chairperson type of approach of consultative government."

Carroll enters Victorian parliament

Carroll won the Niddrie Labor pre-selection battle in 2012 against future cabinet colleague Jaclyn Symes, who is now treasurer.

He then entered Victorian parliament after winning a by-election that was triggered by the resignation of Rob Hulls.

Ben Carroll, Jacinta Allan and Jaclyn Symes following a tour of Parkville Station during construction of the Metro Rail Tunnel in 2025. (AAP Image: Joel Carrett)

Monash University politics professor Zareh Ghazarian said Carroll had held more than a dozen portfolios since Labor returned to power at the 2014 state election, most notably education since 2023.

He became deputy premier under Allan that same year, but not before aiming for the top job himself — a move that reportedly infuriated Andrews, Ghazarian said.

"Ben Carroll attracted some interest as a future leader in the final years of Dan Andrews as premier," he said.

"But he showed significant tenacity in trying to run for the premiership in 2023, despite Dan Andrews's firm, unwavering backing of Jacinta Allan as his successor.

"Andrews wanted Jacinta Allan as premier and Tim Pallas as deputy, but Ben Carroll managed to secure the deputy role and established himself as heir apparent.

"Having said that, Labor's transition from Andrews to Allan was reasonably seamless while the Victorian Liberals have cycled through John Pesutto, Brad Battin and Jess Wilson in less than four years.

"Now Labor will have to deal with the difficulties of leadership change."

Lessons for Carroll ahead of leadership

Carroll has faced several hurdles in the education portfolio, notably the inadvertent release of year 12 exam results and two statewide teacher strikes amid an ongoing pay dispute that showed no sign of being resolved.

Victoria's teachers and education staff have walked off the job twice as part of an unresolved pay dispute. (ABC News: Danielle Bonica)

But Ghazarian said law and order would be the main issue the new Labor leader would need to tackle before polling day, a factor the incoming premier has acknowledged.

"We know, as a 12-year-old government, we have to be the insurgent," Carroll said in early June.

"Focus on the fundamentals: community safety, growing the economy, being a state that's open for business."

Ben Carroll has held multiple portfolios, and is currently education minister. (ABC News)

With social media and populism transforming campaigning in the 2020s, Deane said the Niddrie MP's suburban story could help Labor ahead of the November poll.

"Victoria was traditionally run out of Melbourne's eastern suburbs," he said.

"Bracks and Brumby changed that dynamic. They were very effective in securing Victoria's regional centres during the 2000s, whereas Dan Andrews saw the political potential of Melbourne's outer ring electorates.

" Labor's grip on the type of suburbs Ben represents — north, north-west — were Labor for generations but now stand a real chance of falling to an independent [or] minor party equivalent of what the teal movement has done to the Liberal Party. "

Victoria does not have a history of ditching a premier less than a year out from an election.

Lindsay Thompson was one of Victoria's longest serving parliamentarians but shortest serving premiers, spending only 307 days in the top job from 1981 to 1982. (ABC TV)

The exception is Lindsay Thompson in 1981. Like Mr Carroll, he was an education minister who was thrust into the top job to save the political day.

"Sometimes replacing a premier in an election year works," Ghazarian said.

"There's been examples interstate but, in Victoria, Lindsay Thompson lasted less than 12 months before losing the 1982 election to John Cain."

title: Quick hits: Davies makes history, Diamonds clap back in uni debate
text:
Rose Davies runs a "race of a lifetime" to make Australian history, and the Diamonds remain in the spotlight even off the court.

Here are the quick hits from day four of the Commonwealth Games.

1. Davies makes history on the track

Rose Davies celebrated Australia's first athletics gold of the Games. (Getty Images: Michael Steele)

The eagerly anticipated athletics program finally got underway on the fourth day of competition in Glasgow, and it wasn't long before Australia claimed its first gold on the track.

Rose Davies sat back for much of the women's 10,000m but timed her move to perfection, waiting until less than a kilometre remained before galloping ahead of Kenya's Diana Wanza.

And Davies eventually won in a canter, crossing the finish line almost 11 seconds before silver medallist Wanza.

Australian commentary great Bruce McAvaney called it "the race of a lifetime" during the Network Seven broadcast.

Davies became the first Australian woman to win the 10,000m at a Commonwealth Games.

"These moments come once in a lifetime, and I'm so happy I got to achieve this," Davies told the Seven Network.

2. From a cancer diagnosis to a Games final

Archie Goodburn did not win a medal but won the respect of everyone as he competes while dealing with brain tumours. (Getty Images: SNS Group/Ross MacDonald)

When people say the phrase "there are more important things in life than sport" they're probably speaking about Scotland's Archie Goodburn.

The 25-year-old breaststroke specialist had a chance to compete at the Paris Olympics when he was diagnosed with three inoperable brain tumours in 2024.

But speaking after his race in the final, where he finished seventh, his interview put everything in perspective and made it very hard not to get emotional watching him.

"My dream was to make the final. But outside the pool I dream, like, of a future where brain cancer isn't the biggest killer of those under 40," he said.

"[A dream] where the UK government establish a national brain cancer lead to make that change, and I'd much prefer that that change was made and that dream is completed than any of my personal goals in the pool.

"Because what families and young people are going through out there is really beyond the comprehension of many people out here and certainly far harder than anything I've ever had to do as a world-class sportsman."

3. Welsh sisters twinning in bronze

Abigail Roper won bronze first, but sister Emily got her own an hour or so later. (Getty Images: Naomi Baker)

Wales has not been flush with supreme gymnasts at the Commonwealth Games.

But given their national colour, perhaps it's no surprise that at these Scottish Games that two have come along at once, like lithe, smiling versions of red London buses.

Both Abi Roper and Emily Roper were in action in the vault, with Abi claiming a bronze medal with a score of 13.433, just a fraction ahead of her sister who scored 13.283 after being penalised 0.3 for her landing on her second vault.

Then, an hour or so later, Emily put her disappointment behind her to deliver a display worthy of a medal, also winning bronze behind Australian gold medal winner Katie McDonald.

In a heartening display of sisterly love, Abi could be seen roaring her support from the stands, her own bronze medal dangling around her neck, as her sister delivered the performance of her life to win Wales its first-ever medal on that apparatus at a Commonwealth Games.

"Sometimes we bicker because we are competitive, so we are constantly fighting to see who is better," Emily told a BBC interviewer in 2025.

Who knows how much bickering there would have been had Emily come away from Glasgow empty-handed.

4. Diamonds can't help being icons, even on a day off

After winning their first two matches, our netball world champions had day four off in Glasgow. But everyone's still talking about the Diamonds: just not for the broadcast-related reason you might expect.

Diamonds disappointed first two games only live on streaming service Diamonds fans are disappointed to discover Australia's dominant netball team's Glasgow matches are only being aired live on Seven's online streaming service.

Folks online have been debating Australia's netball uniform, which rides up during play and often ends up looking more like a singlet.

Some are worried the poor design is distracting our goal shooters, who have to take their shots before readjusting the awkward uniform (lest they be penalised for a held ball!).

Currently competing in her third Commonwealth Games, Courtney Bruce has worn a few iterations of the kit over the years, and she says the team isn't too worried about the 2026 uniform.

"It is what it is, there's literally nothing we can do about it, [so] we don't think about it," she told the ABC.

In a video posted on social media Commonwealth Games debutant Sophie Garbin poked fun at what she described as "the most talked about" aspect of the Glasgow event.

She was, however, cleared by a specialist to compete.

"Things might look a little different for me at the Commonwealth Games and Pan Pacs, but I'll give everything I have and do my absolute best every time I race," O'Callaghan said in an Instagram post before the Games.

Some things remained the same though, the Queenslander claiming yet another gold medal for her burgeoning collection in the 200m freestyle and 4x100m freestyle relay.

However, she withdrew from the mixed 4x100m freestyle relay and did not line up in the 50m backstroke heats on Monday morning to focus on the 100m freestyle final that evening.

title: Plan to return Hobart land to Aboriginal group gets council support
text:
An Aboriginal land return proposal near Hobart's CBD has passed its first hurdle after receiving "in-principle support" at a Hobart City Council meeting.

The 4.9-hectare parcel of land near the summit of Queens Domain was identified by the council last year as a possible site for an Indigenous-owned cultural centre operated by the Tasmanian Aboriginal Centre (TAC).

Lord Mayor Anna Reynolds said Monday's motion, which passed nine votes to three, had "strong support around the table".

Councillor Reynolds said those who voted against the proposal had raised procedural questions, including whether the hand back could be blocked at a later stage.

"If we had a state government who did not want this to happen, roadblocks could be put in place," Cr Reynolds said.

"But we've heard from the Minister for Aboriginal Affairs, Bridget Archer … and we know that she sees this as a good idea.

"Whether that process is smooth or takes a really long time is really incumbent on all the partners on this journey. This includes the council, but it is also the state government and all their different departments, and also the Aboriginal Land Council."

Hobart Lord Mayor Anna Reynolds says the motion passed 9 votes to 3. (ABC News: Luke Bowden)

The vote was not the final approval for the land return but will allow the council's chief executive to undertake the necessary work to progress the proposal, which includes investigating any title issues for subdivision, and obtaining legal, planning, heritage, environmental and land tenure advice.

A development application and public consultation would still need to be completed, and any cultural centre would be subject to a separate future development application.

The earmarked area is currently classified as public land and the council-proposed subdivision would not impact the public's access to it.

This parcel contains an area suitable for development alongside part of the lowland native grassland. (ABC News: Andrew Cunningham)

'Unique opportunity' for establishing cultural centre

Loading...

If approved, the land parcel off Domain Road would be Tasmania's first Aboriginal land return in more than two decades.

Aboriginal Land Council of Tasmania (ALCT) general manager Sarah Wilcox said the transfer would be welcomed by the community.

"This is a really unique opportunity to think about establishing a cultural centre which can serve as a keeping place," she said.

" Currently in the Aboriginal community, we have absolutely nowhere to look after our sacred cultural items. "

If it gets final approval, it would be the first Aboriginal land handback in Tasmania in more than 20 years. (ABC News: Andrew Cunningham)

In its proposal, the council report referenced ALCT chair Greg Brown, who said the cultural centre would create "spaces for interpretation, exhibition, and the sharing of stories by Aboriginal artists and cultural practitioners".

"For us as Palawa people, serving our community and caring for Country is a profound responsibility and privilege," he said.

"Since 1995, the return of land has enabled meaningful cultural, social and economic outcomes for our people; outcomes that are only possible through strong, respectful relationships with government and the broader Tasmanian community."

The ALCT has proposed a collaborative land management arrangement with the council to share "ongoing stewardship of the broader Queens Domain".

'A lot of red tape'

Cr Reynolds said the transfer of the council-owned land would be fairly involved with much "state government red tape".

'People do care': Why private owners are handing land back It has been two decades since substantial land hand-backs in Tasmania, so private owners are doing it instead.

"We still have to go through quite a lot of process," she said.

"We have to go through a separate process to close off a bit of Domain Road so we can access that asphalt space. We have to rehabilitate it. We also then have to go through a disposal of public land process, which is quite involved."

The council was asked by the TAC last year for support to build an Aboriginal-owned and operated cultural centre in the state's capital.

The centre would host cultural items, act as a performance space and support Aboriginal food enterprises and other tourism activities.

There have been no large-scale land returns in Tasmania since 2005, when Truwana/Cape Barren Island and Lungtalanana/Clarke Island were returned to the ALCT.

title: Savannah Guthrie pleads with mother's kidnappers to 'help us find her'
text:
NBC's Today show co-host Savannah Guthrie says her family is living an unending nightmare nearly six months after her mother's disappearance, pleading with her kidnappers to "tell us where to look for her".

A video released on Monday, local time, is the latest public plea from the journalist since Nancy Guthrie, 84, disappeared from her home just outside Tucson, Arizona on February 1.

She said her family would never stop looking for her.

"The world can be a cruel and unforgiving place, and I know that you have tried to do things the right way," she said.

"So I'm asking you, begging you, to do the right thing now. Make the right choice. Help us find her. Tell us where to look for her. I truly believe it is never too late to do the right thing."

Loading Instagram content

Authorities believe Nancy Guthrie was taken against her will on February 1.

They found blood near the front doorstep of her home just outside Tucson, and the FBI later released surveillance videos showing a masked man on the porch that night.

Volunteers and search teams scoured nearby desert terrain filled with cactuses, bushes and boulders in the weeks after she vanished.

A volunteer group recently searched for her body near the Arizona-Mexico border.

It has been four months since Nancy Guthrie vanished It has been four months since Nancy Guthrie, the mother of America's Today show co-host Savannah Guthrie, was reported missing.

Three notes gained wide attention

Authorities have not said how many purported ransom demands were made after Nancy Guthrie's disappearance, though three news organisations reported receiving such notes and turned them over to investigators.

The FBI has discounted some of the ransom notes as nothing more than extortion attempts, but said it was still evaluating others that might be legitimate.

The federal agency hasn't specified which ransom notes might be genuine.

The US television personality has previously made a series of social media posts about her mother after she went missing.

In the days after the disappearance, the broadcaster and her siblings acknowledged they were aware of media reports of a supposed ransom letter and were ready to talk and listen, but wanted proof their mother was alive.

Weeks later, Savannah Guthrie said her family was offering a $US1 million ($1.45 million) reward for information leading to the recovery of her mother.

She also acknowledged for the first time that her mother might not be alive, but added that there was still hope.

title: Regional NSW council cuts services as it weighs 42pc rate hike
text:
Albury councillors have voted six-two to reduce opening hours at some of the regional New South Wales city's facilities and make its Visitor Information Centre unstaffed as the council works to address a multi-million-dollar budget deficit.

The changes, approved at last night's meeting, form part of the council's Financial Sustainability Program, which aims to reduce costs.

The measures will see the Visitor Information Centre at the LibraryMuseum become unstaffed, reduced opening hours at Lavington Library and the Murray Art Museum Albury (MAMA) close on Mondays.

The changes are expected to save about $110,000 a year.

Councillors voted six-two in favour of the changes, which include reducing opening hours at the art museum. (ABC News: Gaye Pattison)

The service reductions come as councillors consider whether to apply to the NSW Independent Pricing and Regulatory Tribunal (IPART) for a Special Rate Variation (SRV), with options of a 40 per cent increase over three years, or a 42 per cent increase over two years.

Any increase would require IPART approval before taking effect.

An update on the Financial Sustainability Program before councillors last night said the council had reduced its projected General Fund deficit from more than $22 million in late 2025 to $18.9 million.

The meeting heard council had delivered about $1.6 million in ongoing savings with a potential further $3.3 million in savings through changes to services, property management and day-to-day operations.

Mayor Kevin Mack has encouraged the entire Albury community to have their say on a possible 42 per cent rate increase over two years. (ABC Goulburn Murray: Philippe Perez)

Councillor Darren Cameron, who voted against the motion, said the measures did not go far enough.

"In my view we're only dabbling with the measures that have been taken so far," he said.

"We have to reconcile ourselves to the fact that we are going to have to massively reduce services if we are going to avoid a SRV."

Cr Cameron said he believed council should consider more significant service reductions, including placing MAMA into care and maintenance until the city's financial position improved.

Councillor Stuart Baker, who supported the motion, said there was no simple solution to the council's financial challenges.

"I am having trouble seeing an easy path that Albury City can get out of it," he said.

"We can't get out of it by just cutting everything and reducing services because then Albury isn't the way we want it to be.

" People come here and live here because it is a good place to live, work and do business and bring up families. "

Albury will be one of the most expensive councils in terms of household rates in NSW if it seeks a Special Rate Variation. (ABC News: Ashlee Aldridge)

Speaking during the public forum, Albury Ratepayers Association spokesperson Susan Keighran said the group was "representing a large number of the community that are deeply concerned about the proposed SRV".

"My primary concern is that Albury City Council has shifted the financial burden primarily onto ratepayers without first exhausting internal structural reforms," she said.

"I appreciate that managing a growing city like ours involves difficult decisions and I don't underestimate that responsibility for a second."

Ms Keighran said many residents were already struggling with rising living costs.

Albury City Council is considering a rate rise of up to 42 per cent over the next two years. (ABC News: Ashlee Aldridge)

Ms Keighran said the association believed council should continue looking for savings before asking residents to pay higher rates.

"We, the community, are asking council to look within themselves, sort out your own back of house, balance incoming funds with affordable projects and trim some financial fat," she said.

"We, the ratepayers and renters that make up this wonderful community, should not be expected to be a bank for Albury City."

She said higher rates would also affect local businesses as households reduced spending on dining out, entertainment and other discretionary purchases.

Community consultation on the proposed SRV closes on July 31. Councillors are expected to consider the feedback before deciding whether to lodge an application with IPART.

title: Oscar-winning composer brings Icelandic poetry to Australian stages
text:
It's not every day that an Oscar-winning composer writes new music for an Australian orchestra. But that's exactly what happened with the Australian Chamber Orchestra's latest commission.

Hildur Guðnadóttir has composed a new piece for the orchestra, in collaboration with Norwegian trumpeter Arve Henriksen and vocal ensemble Trio Mediæval.

In 2020, Guðnadóttir made history as one of the few female composers to win an Oscar. Her score for Joker also earned her a Golden Globe and a BAFTA.

Hildur Guðnadóttir's Oscar win in 2020 inspired female composers around the world. (Getty Images: Kevin Winter)

Her work on the miniseries Chernobyl also won a BAFTA, a Grammy and an Emmy.

"It was a bit of a shock that came with such a bang," Guðnadóttir says about her wins.

" I didn't grow up dreaming about winning an Oscar one day because that just simply wasn't in any of my horizon. "

Already an established composer, the awards opened more doors for Guðnadóttir, who currently lives in Berlin.

Since 2020, she has released two solo studio albums and four major film soundtracks, among other projects.

The land of ice and fire

Guðnadóttir grew up in Iceland, the island nation known for its northern lights, volcanoes and ancient Viking sagas.

Despite Iceland's well-known storytelling tradition, classical music is relatively new, according to Guðnadóttir.

"We don't have a long history of music because music was banned in Iceland for such a long time," she explains, adding "it was banned because of religion".

The first concert by a full symphony orchestra in Iceland didn't happen until 1926, when the Hamburg Philharmonic came to its capital city Reykjavík.

Storytelling survived through rimur, which Guðnadóttir says is "a way of reciting poetry or singing in this tremolo, a bit like imitating the sound that sheep make".

"Our weather and our living situation were pretty rough for quite a long time, and we lived in dirt houses up until not so long ago," she says.

"When I was growing up, we had very limited resources: very little access to physical records, and a limited amount of amplifiers and microphones. So, we've kind of been a nation of just making do with what we have."

That resourcefulness has shaped Iceland's music scene, transforming rugged landscapes and a long storytelling tradition into everything from chart-topping songs by artists such as Björk to genre-defying experimental music, with Guðnadóttir at its forefront.

Writing for an Australian orchestra

During the current tour, the Australian Chamber Orchestra premiered Guðnadóttir's new work, Time and the Water.

The Australian Chamber Orchestra performs Guðnadóttir's Time and the Water during its national tour. (Supplied: Australian Chamber Orchestra)

The commission came through her connection with Arve Henriksen, who is touring with the orchestra alongside Trio Mediæval.

The music is based on Tíminn og Vatnið (Time and the Water), a poem by modernist Icelandic poet Steinn Steinarr.

"Both of my grandmothers used to recite Steinarr's poems to me because they were both big lovers of poetry," Guðnadóttir says.

The poem explores separation and connection between lovers through water, an image that resonates deeply with Guðnadóttir.

"Living in Berlin, I really miss being close to the sea," she says.

For the orchestra, performing a new work by Guðnadóttir is "a real coup", says executive producer Ross McHenry.

Guðnadóttir's music is presented as part of a concert program that weaves together ancient Nordic medieval hymns and the atmospheric post‑rock sound of Icelandic band Sigur Rós.

McHenry describes the program, crafted for what he calls "the racehorse of the world's great string orchestras", as an exploration of extreme beauty.

The Australian Chamber Orchestra, featuring violinist Satu Vänskä, is widely regarded as one of the world's leading ensembles. (Supplied: Australian Chamber Orchestra)

He draws a connection between the music and the landscapes that inspired it.

"There's this thing about these places," he says.

"Whether it's Iceland, northern Sweden, or even the central desert here in Australia: they're stark, but they're also incredibly beautiful."

What Australia can learn from Iceland

Guðnadóttir's historic Oscar win has inspired composers around the world, including Australian screen composer Caitlin Yeo.

An award‑winning composer herself, Yeo reflects on the impact of witnessing Guðnadóttir's triumph.

"When a woman gets up to pick up one of those gold statues, it's incredibly significant, given the dire under‑representation of women in the screen industry," she says.

" If we can see it, we can be it. "

The similarities between Iceland and Australia go beyond dramatic landscapes.

Both countries are geographically isolated, and both are prone to climates that seem designed to test human endurance.

Iceland is also famous for having roads that wouldn't exactly win international awards.

But Yeo reflects on how Iceland treasures its artists: "It sounds like it was very precious to make music in the first place, and they look after it like a gem."

One of Iceland's initiatives to support musicians is through a monthly artist salary fund.

While Australian musicians are making waves internationally, Yeo says support at home can be inconsistent.

Caitlin Yeo believes Australia can become a music powerhouse with stronger support and more collaboration between artists. (Caitlin Yeo: Damian de Boos-Smith)

"At the moment, there's just less work out there, and the film and TV industry particularly is reverting to risk‑averse behaviour," she says, adding this trend has been a global phenomenon.

"What that means is that they're less likely to hire a gender‑diverse composer at the end of the day."

Guðnadóttir attributes much of her success to Iceland's tight‑knit creative community.

"With our limited resources comes a lot of just figuring things out and helping each other out," she says.

"There's not really any sense of rivalry and competition. We're all very happy for each other when someone does well."

Yeo believes Australia could benefit from a similar approach.

"If artists advocate for each other, work together, collaborate, and pool our resources, we could be an absolute powerhouse too," Yeo says.

As for Iceland's genre‑defying musical identity, Guðnadóttir offers a simple explanation:

" We're just so few, everyone is playing for everybody. So, I think that's why we have this sense of genres not being so important. "

Reserve Bank governor Michele Bullock has put an interest rate hike on the agenda for the bank’s August meeting while warning that without a lift in productivity, Australians will struggle to get real wage increases. In just her second formal speech of the year, Bullock told a charity event in Sydney today that while there were signs inflation had not lifted as high as feared following the surge in oil prices, it remained too high. text:

Breaking BusinessCompaniesAdvertising Gerry Harvey branded the legal system unjust. It has come back to bite him Elias Visontay July 28, 2026 — 12:38pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A judge has singled out comments from billionaire retailer Gerry Harvey calling the legal system “f---ed” as a factor in slapping his company Harvey Norman with $35 million in penalties for running misleading ads. On Tuesday, Justice Michael O’Bryan made the orders against both Harvey Norman and credit company Latitude Finance Australia – which must pay $20 million in penalties – over a misleading and deceptive advertising campaign spruiking the latter’s credit card product. Harvey Norman chairman Gerry Harvey arriving at Lachlan Murdoch’s annual Christmas party in Sydney’s Bellevue Hill in December. Oscar Colman The Australian Securities and Investments Commission (ASIC) had taken Harvey Norman and Latitude to court over a national ad campaign that ran between January 2020 and August 2021, which promoted products as available via a “no-deposit” and 60-month interest-free payment method. But it failed to disclose that customers were actually required to sign up for a credit card with high establishment and monthly fees to access the deal. In October 2024, the Federal Court found the companies had misled people with the ads, saying customers entered a “fundamentally different financial arrangement” than the one promoted. An appeal by Harvey Norman and Latitude was dismissed in September 2025.

Advertisement

In delivering his decision on penalties, O’Bryan highlighted how Harvey Norman and Latitude responded to the case in significantly different ways. “Neither company had a suitable process for ensuring that their advertising complied with the consumer protection laws. Given the scale and sophistication of both defendants, that is an extraordinary state of affairs,” O’Bryan said. He said it was “particularly striking in the case of Harvey Norman, given the size of the company”. He added that while Latitude had since provided “evidence of the steps that it has now taken to improve its processes in that regard”, Harvey Norman failed to do so. “That is a distinguishing feature between the two defendants, relatedly, the defendants have also exhibited a different level of contrition,” O’Bryan said. “Latitude’s general counsel offered an apology to Latitude’s customers on behalf of the company.

Advertisement

Related Article Retail ‘We all get hammered’: Harvey Norman’s court battles don’t faze Gerry “In contrast, no executive or legal counsel of Harvey Norman gave evidence about the company’s compliance procedures or offered an apology, and public statements made by Harvey Norman’s chairman show a disregard for the potential harm suffered by consumers from Harvey Norman’s misleading conduct.” A month after the court’s initial 2024 decision, the retailer’s namesake, Gerry Harvey, declined to specifically discuss the case and said his lawyers did not want him talking about the topic, but he unleashed on the legal system as a whole. “If I had my way, I’d be out there screaming at the top of my lungs about the injustices, and yet I can’t do it. I’ve got to play along with it,” he told this masthead at the time. “The whole legal system is completely f---ed in Australia.” O’Bryan said that taking into account those considerations had led him to decide more significant penalties for Harvey Norman. “A higher penalty is warranted to deter repetition and to motivate Harvey Norman to improve its compliance processes,” he said.

Advertisement

Harvey, who was contacted by phone for comment on Tuesday, downplayed his involvement in the company, which is now run by his wife Katie Page as chief executive. “I used to sell fridges, but now I’m a farmer,” Harvey said. In the full judgment, O’Bryan was scathing of Harvey’s comments: “Mr Harvey is entitled to express his opinions, including about the legal system. However, Mr Harvey’s opinions indicate that the Chairman of Harvey Norman’s sole focus is upon the perceived injustice suffered by Harvey Norman, and a complete disregard for the potential harm suffered by consumers from Harvey Norman’s misleading conduct.” “Taking the evidence as a whole, I am not persuaded that Harvey Norman has demonstrated any contrition for its wrongful conduct,” O’Bryan said. O’Bryan also said that while the quantifiable harm to consumers was likely less than $5 million, consumers may have wasted their time investigating the offer, or become so invested before realising its true terms that they ultimately proceeded. As such, he estimated the incremental revenue earned by each party through the contravening conduct was about $5 million.

Advertisement

Both Harvey Norman and Latitude will also have to publish notices on their websites about the orders for 90 days, and pay ASIC’s costs. ASIC had been seeking penalties of $50 million against Harvey Norman and $35 million against Latitude, as well as injunctions restraining the companies from advertising similar deals for five years, which O’Bryan did not order. text:
Jacinta Allan’s exit speech focused heavily on her decades of achievement, but the Commonwealth Games and Big Build corruption were glaring omissions. This feature looks past the official farewell to examine the frustration, the failures and the fault lines of her premiership.

In Glasgow, Australian athletes have dominated the 2026 Commonwealth Games medal table – a success Premier Jacinta Allan was once supposed to bask in. But their glory ended up taking place far away from her. Instead, Allan was attempting to fend off a leadership challenge from colleagues despairing at Labor’s bleak prospects of retaining power in November’s state election. The government’s disastrous, and some might say farcical, decision to withdraw as host of the games just months before Allan became leader eliminated any prospect of political gain Labor might have hoped for from the event. That decision, along with Allan’s role as minister for Commonwealth Games delivery – among her many other senior portfolios before taking the reins as premier – helped lay the groundwork for this week’s coup, which ultimately saw Victoria’s second female premier resign on Tuesday morning. In her resignation speech, Victorians saw the emotional range that Allan carried as she reflected on her legacy. Her time was up, but she insisted she was not done fighting. Through tears and smiles and trademark defiance, Allan spoke about her many achievements. She thanked her supporters, but her voice wavered when speaking of the many moments with her family she had sacrificed. “I would have absolutely relished the fight this November. I was more than ready.” Jacinta Allan, exit speech

Advertisement

There were many omissions, most importantly when it came to Big Build corruption and of course the Commonwealth Games. Girl, interrupted: Jacinta Allan arrives to relinquish the premiership. Jason South In 2022, together with then premier Daniel Andrews, Allan promised a boon for the regions where they planned to stage the games. At the time, the Andrews government’s ascendancy mirrored the Australian swimming team’s current performance – easily dominating its middling rivals at the games in Glasgow. New housing and sports venues. Jobs. Invaluable attention on the world stage. Business and cultural opportunities. The government spruiked these selling points at every opportunity. Jacinta Allan at a level crossing removal in 2016, when she was public transport minister. Eddie Jim The decision to abruptly withdraw as host invited ridicule after such grandiose promises, and the games quickly became a symbol of the political baggage the government had accumulated over three imposing terms in power. When Andrews resigned as premier in September 2023, that burden became Allan’s to carry. She never seemed to free herself from its weight.

Advertisement

In a cruel twist of fate, some of Allan’s greatest ministerial achievements added significantly to her undoing. After Labor’s return to office at the 2014 election, Allan held some of the most senior and prominent portfolios in the government, including transport and infrastructure, priority precincts, major projects and the Suburban Rail Loop. Daniel Andrews and Jacinta Allan on a tour of the new Town Hall Station, part of the Metro Tunnel project, in 2022. Nicki Connolly On Tuesday, Allan gave profuse thanks for the opportunity to see projects including the Metro Tunnel through to completion. “They are not just projects; they are assets that will improve our lives.” Jactina Allan, exit speech Her successful leadership in the level crossing removal program provided the Andrews government with a weapon they used to clobber political opponents. Andrews and Allan traversed the city to “apologise for the progress we’re making” with their infrastructure projects. They turned the inconvenience of construction works into a real-time billboard for their city-building agenda. Every disruption, train replacement bus and even compulsory property acquisitions became deftly wielded political advantages.

Advertisement

She always seemed to be at Andrews’ side during infrastructure press conferences, high-vis vests and hard hats reinforcing visually their commitment to working for Victoria. They carried away boom gates, inspected underground works on the Metro Tunnel and stood beside the routes for planned roads, while the opposition floundered in relative anonymity. These projects – as well as the West Gate Tunnel, Regional Rail Revival, Melbourne Airport Rail and North East Link – came to be known as the Big Build. “Thank you to Daniel Andrews, who taught us to put people first” Jactina Allan, exit speech But through all those media appearances, Andrews was the undeniable star of the show. Allan had a strong command of the government’s many projects and their mechanics and complexities. Yet Andrews’ authoritative presence gave little chance for his colleague to truly shine. Before her retirement from politics in 2022, some political observers had expected it would be Jill Hennessy – Allan’s factional ally from the Left – who would take over from Andrews.

Advertisement

When it came to charming the press pack on tour buses during election campaigns or explaining emotionally complex policies, including the government’s voluntary assisted dying reforms, Hennessy was a star performer. She had the kind of warm and common touch in media appearances that Allan lacked. Yet, even if Allan had been a stronger media performer, there was no way of spinning the corruption and cost overruns that plagued the projects for which she was responsible. Revelations published by The Age of organised crime inflating the cost of the government’s infrastructure agenda to the tune of billions of dollars dealt a devastating blow to Allan’s credibility. Reporting by investigative journalist Nick McKenzie that Mick Gatto was benefiting from the Big Build caught public attention in a way that few news stories can. Victorians across the state were outraged that gangland figures were profiting at the public’s expense while their roads lay riddled with tyre-popping potholes. Like the government’s handling of the botched Commonwealth Games bid, Allan had no way of claiming plausible deniability about the cost overruns and organised crime presence. It all happened on her watch. Premier Jacinta Allan has rejected multiple calls for a royal commission into corruption on the Big Build. Eddie Jim

title: We might be sitting on a $2,600,000,000,000,000 bomb
text:

BusinessThe economyGlobal economy Opinion We might be sitting on a $2,600,000,000,000,000 bomb Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist July 28, 2026 — 11:57am

July 28, 2026 — 11:57am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Global wealth is booming, but it is on increasingly shaky foundations. Last week the McKinsey Global Institute issued its annual global balance sheet. It estimated that global wealth hit almost $US1.8 quadrillion ($2.6 quadrillion, with a quadrillion equalling a thousand trillion) last year. In 2024, it was $US1.7 quadrillion. McKinsey’s annual report warned that increases in wealth are being driven by paper gains, rather than by real economic growth. AP While that might be regarded as an indicator of an increasingly prosperous world, McKinsey referred to the “mounting detachment” of the balance sheet from the global economy, with several asset classes growing further out of balance with the underlying growing economy. Essentially, it is saying that most of the increases in wealth are being driven by paper gains, rather than by real economic growth.

Advertisement

It singled out US equities, where values “soared” to 2.4 times corporate net assets, with profits double their share of GDP relative to their shares in 2000. China’s corporate debt, it said, grew to 80 per cent of real assets against a global average of 50 per cent, while government debt was near all-time highs in the US and was growing most rapidly in China. Related Article Luxury property Where Australia’s richest people live and how much it costs to live there Of the global increase in household wealth to $US570 trillion, only 20 per cent came from real capital formation – new investment in machinery and equipment, buildings, infrastructure and intellectual property – with valuations of existing assets growing 4 percentage points faster than already high consumer price inflation. It is valuations and inflation driving the balance sheet expansion, not economic growth. Macquarie Capital’s Viktor Shvets has long spoken and written about “hyper-financialisation” and “a cloud of finance” in which the growth of financial assets far outstrips, and is disconnected from, real economies.

Advertisement

He’s also written of what he calls the “Fujiwara effect” (when several hurricanes merge), or the fusion of deep financialisation with a disruptive acceleration of the Information Age. The coincidence of financialisation and technological advancement, he has argued, generates an over accumulation of capital, displacement of labour by technology, rising inequality and social tensions and intense disinflation. The largest asset class within the McKinsey balance sheet is real estate, where values (except in Australia, at least until very recently) have been correcting relative to GDP. Louie Douvis McKinsey detailed the implications of a balance sheet outrunning the underlying economy, and there are echoes of Shvets’ view of the world in its conclusions. When real estate and equity values rise faster than GDP, it says, weaknesses can be exposed, capital can flow disproportionately to asset repurchases, sometimes with a lot of leverage and while, valuations might rise, the real economy might be deprived of the investment that drives long-term growth.

Advertisement

“For households, wealth rises but merely on paper, with heightened risk of eventual corrections. Growing asset values also tend to exacerbate wealth inequality, as existing owners of wealth see large gains while entering asset markets becomes harder for others.” Related Article Opinion

Elon Musk Before we build a statue of Elon Musk, let’s consider what he’s done with his trillions of dollars Shane Wright Senior economics correspondent It nominates three ways in which an overly inflated balance sheet might correct. One, the most benign, is with productivity-driven growth in the real economy that boosts income to validate high asset valuations and high levels of debt. Artificial intelligence holds out that promise, although at present it is probably doing more to exacerbate asset values and leverage than to increase productivity and boost real income.

Advertisement

The other two options aren’t as palatable. Sustained inflation would erode the real value of assets and debt while producing higher nominal GDP while a balance sheet “reset” – a sharp drop in asset values, significant deleveraging, corporate and personal defaults, losses of wealth and employment and lower economic growth – would also shrink the balance sheet. Macquarie Capital’s Viktor Shvets has long spoken and written about “hyper-financialisation ” and “a cloud of finance” in which the growth of financial assets far outstrips, and is disconnected from, real economies. Dion Georgopoulos That’s what happened when the dot-com bubble burst in 2000, and when the global financial crisis occurred in 2008. An abrupt shrinking of the global balance sheet to realign it with the underlying global economy would, as it was in those past instances, be traumatic. The world could, of course, just muddle along with the kind of stagnation that developed during the period after the 2008 global financial crisis, with low growth, low interest rates, low investment and increasing leverage, although it is hard to see how that could be a sustainable condition.

Advertisement

A breakdown of trends within the McKinsey balance sheet shows equity is now 2.8 times global GDP, against an average of 1.9 times over the preceding 24 years since 2000. Government debt, at 0.9 per cent of GDP, has edged up from 0.8 times and corporate debt has done the same. Household debt has edged down from 0.8 to 0.7 times, while currency and deposits have risen from 1.5 times GDP to 1.7 times. “Growing asset values also tend to exacerbate wealth inequality, as existing owners of wealth see large gains while entering asset markets becomes harder for others.” McKinsey report The largest asset class within the balance sheet is real estate, where values (except in Australia, at least until very recently) have been correcting relative to GDP, and the second-largest is equity, where values relative to GDP are at all-time highs in some countries.

Advertisement

That’s most notably the case in the US, which accounts for nearly half of the total of global equity and where equity values are 2.4 times net assets. In most other countries they are around 1 times net assets. The other big element in the balance sheet is debt, where household debt has been trending down, but corporate debt in China has nearly doubled the global average, and government debt – relative to GDP – had the fastest growth. Government debt was above 100 per cent of GDP in Japan, the US, Italy, France, Canada, Belgium, Spain and the UK. Government debt was near all-time highs in the US and was growing most rapidly in China. Bloomberg In the US, massive deficits, debt levels that are swelling inexorably, inflation and rising bond yields are raising threat levels while in other parts of the world unbalanced or weak growth, when combined with high levels of government debt, also threaten. The world’s two key economies – the US and China – face different challenges. The US needs to consume less and save more, while China needs to save less and consume more (and perhaps invest more productively).

Advertisement

Related Article Opinion

Trade wars Trump’s America is sinking as his war on the world sputters Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist The best-case scenario is for artificial intelligence to deliver, benignly, on its promise of a leap change in productivity, although how those benefits, if they do emerge, are shared will have profound social implications. The world doesn’t need – and probably wouldn’t tolerate – the wealth from those productivity gains being captured by a handful of trillionaires. It remains plausible, however, that an AI sector that is still in a development phase and built on access to equity at ever-inflating valuations and access to ever-increasing amounts of cheap debt won’t reach a level of maturity, with positive cashflows and maybe even actual earnings, before investors run out of patience or capacity to support it. That’s the year-2000 scenario, which would be a setback, albeit not necessarily a permanent one, for a productivity-led resetting/rescue of a global balance sheet that, on McKinsey’s analysis, appears vulnerable and, perhaps, unsustainable. Lo Presti’s is an “unassumingly delicious” new restaurant overlooking Redfern Park, opened by former Baba’s Place head chef Michael Lo Presti and restaurant manager Rachael Trewin. “It’s not going to look flashy, but there’s going to be a lot of care in what we do,” said Lo Presti, of the Mediterranean-leaning menu featuring grilled pork with local pipis, ling wrapped in vine leaves, and an avgolemono sour cocktail, inspired by the Greek lemon chicken soup. 1 / 7 Owners Rachael Trewin and chef Michael Lo Presti. It’s a two-storey corner terrace, with one of Lo Presti’s father Greg’s old sketches repurposed into an illuminated sign out front. Opening a restaurant of his own was always part of the plan, Lo Presti said. He grew up in the family’s Darlinghurst restaurant of the same name and watched as regulars became friends.

Lo Presti went on to three-hatted Stanmore restaurant Sixpenny, and was a finalist in The Sydney Morning Herald Good Food Guide 2024 Young Chef of the Year award. Their friendship endured, and for the past two years they worked alongside each other at hatted Marrickville restaurant Baba’s Place. They’d always talked about wanting to open a place of their own, somewhere they’d want to go for dinner themselves, said Lo Presti. It made sense to do it together.

“I went on holiday down to Melbourne and Tasmania and I saw all these small, independently run restaurants and I’m like … I think it’s time, now, to do it myself,” he said. “It’s getting harder and harder these days to open up an independent restaurant and we thought we’d just get our foot in the door.” Lo Presti’s is designed to make diners feel like “you’re coming over to someone’s house for a dinner party”. Dion Georgopoulos The goal was to create a warm, inviting space where diners could just as well walk in for a glass of Montepulciano at the bar, or book ahead for a relaxed Sunday lunch on the terrace. “I want it to feel like you’re coming over to someone’s house for a dinner party, but it’s actually a functioning restaurant,” Trewin said.

The menu is deliberately understated. A plate of roasted capsicum is dehydrated, just slightly (“so it’s a little bit chewier and the flavours are fortified”), and dressed simply with Pedro Ximenez vinegar. Braised kangaroo tail, swaps oxtail for “such an underutilised cut”, marinated overnight in an “almost-Caribbean style” spice blend, then braised until it’s “sticky, rich and dark”, served with salsa. Hanger steak. Dion Georgopoulos “It’s rich, but there’s respite in that dish with salsa and fresh mint,” Lo Presti said. The wine list stays predominantly local, offering a range of price points, with a rotating option imported from Europe.

“We want it to be a warm, comfortable place … but fun, a little bit loud, with a lot of regulars … you know, you come in, you sit in the same spot, we know what you like,” Lo Presti said. “I think it will be the kind of place where people come in and feel like they’re contributing something to the restaurant, like they’re part of something, because customers really do contribute.” Open lunch Sat-Sun; dinner Thu-Sat Level 1, 34b Redfern Street, Redfern (entrance via Elizabeth Street), loprestisrestaurant.com
