Washington: If you’re feeling a touch sorry for yourself, Alex De Minaur can recommend a cure - get married. The 27-year-old from Sydney wedded fellow tennis star Katie Boulter just after Wimbledon, a tournament he exited in a disappointing round of 16 loss to Italy’s Flavio Cobolli. By his own admission, De Minaur was beating himself up. Alex de Minaur on his wedding day. Kate Julia “It breaks me inside. That’s the reality of it,” he said at the time. “Many, many hours get put into my craft, and countless years, to have moments like these. To not step up to the plate is truly gut-wrenching.” But the wedding - first an intimate ceremony in England, then a larger celebration in Tuscany, and a very brief honeymoon in Portofino - has helped cast those blues aside, and recharge the batteries.

Advertisement

“We did the maths, it’s probably the longest I’ve ever had without touching a racquet,” he says on the sidelines of the Mubadala DC Open in Washington. “It was probably about 13 days.” Thirteen days is a veritable eternity in the hectic schedule of professional tennis, which De Minaur thinks should be shortened. On Sunday, he talked about needing a break around this time of year, after the Roland Garros-Wimbledon double act and before the lead-up to the US Open. Alex de Minaur and Katie Boulter on their wedding day. Kate Julia De Minaur doesn’t regret baring his soul in the aftermath of his Wimbledon defeat, but he feels it was overblown. His raw post-match news conference, in which he seemed on the verge of tears, received a lot of attention. “I don’t think it was warranted, as much as - myself included - a lot of people wanted to make a big deal out of it,” he says now.

“It became a really big thing, but realistically it took me a couple of days to get over it. It was just the same feelings and emotions that any athlete has after a tough loss. Now I’m feeling great.” De Minaur points out that he may have suffered disappointing losses on the big stages in Paris and London, but he is now at a career high ranking of world No. 5. “That’s not too shabby,” he says. His challenge is to channel that success into mental resilience on court – as he says, to play more freely and “with a little bit less weight on my shoulders”. The burden of expectation is heavy these days. Does he feel pressure to win from the Australian tennis public? “It mainly comes from myself,” he says. “As you win more matches, as you get closer to the top, more and more people have opinions on you than they did 10 years ago … It just comes with the job. “In fact, it’s a good thing. I’ve earned the right for people to have opinions about myself and my tennis. Whether they’re right or wrong, or whether they just want to have clickbait articles or not, that’s something else. Australia’s largest electricity and gas retailer has confirmed that the personal information of about 900,000 current and former customers was hacked in a major cybersecurity incident. If opposition leader is the most unenviable job in politics, then Nationals leader in opposition has to be a close second. Gurmesh Singh, a Coffs Harbour macadamia and blueberry farmer-turned-politician, was elevated to that position in November last year. Along with Liberal leader Kellie Sloane, who gained office only days later, he became a newly minted political leader just weeks before the country’s worst-ever terror attack. Now he’s the man tasked with saving his party’s regional NSW seats from a One Nation avalanche at next year’s election. He’s also the first Sikh elected to an Australian parliament and the first Sikh leader of a major party. He has a rich family history, and a portrait of Singh’s great-grandfather is plastered on walls around the country. When we sit down to lunch on a rainy Sydney Tuesday, One Nation has been surging in the polls, and most of the talk on Macquarie Street about the Nationals often concludes with something like “they’re in major trouble”. I know it’s probably not what Singh wants me to talk about but I can’t help but ask how he feels about Pauline Hanson’s surge in popularity and her calls for a monoculture, given his own background. “I grew up in the ’80s and ’90s in what we would describe as Australian culture, in what some of these people are saying they’d like us to be,” he says. “It’s a good culture that I would also like to live in again. “I look at myself [and my family] – we’ve got a different ethnicity, obviously we have different religious beliefs, and we might have slightly different festivals and religious celebrations, but I think you can do that while still being uniquely Australian as well, and I think that’s the more mature conversation that we should be having … how do we – and you can – do both.”

Advertisement

“I think what people are actually looking for is what we had back then. That’s safer streets, that was an economy that meant you could have a house with one income, it meant kids who were out on their bikes, meant you could go to the beach on a weekend – like, these are the things that people remember … It’s actually things that government should be striving for, right?” The most recent Resolve Political Monitor conducted over June and July found support for the Coalition at the lowest in recent memory, down to 23 per cent and trailing behind One Nation, which sat at 25 per cent despite not yet having a single endorsed candidate for the NSW election. Singh says he believes the tides will turn in the time between now and the March poll, and that Coalition policies like a reduction in payroll tax, released earlier than usual in this election cycle, will get people back on board with the core Nationals principles of smaller governments and better infrastructure for the bush. Related Article Editorial

Resolve Political Monitor NSW voters revolt against major parties The Herald's View Editorial We’re lunching at Matt Moran’s Chophouse in Sydney’s CBD, a sophisticated steak house a short walk from Parliament House where Singh is familiar with the menu. He has a secret passion for hot chips, a love so deep that in his younger years he tried his hand at building an online map of his best reviewed offerings in Sydney. The chips at Chophouse and Bondi’s Hotel Ravesis are up there among the best, he says, but so are those from parliament’s Long Bell Cafe. (I share this enthusiasm and am all too familiar with the salty, crunchy goodness, given the kitchen is mere steps from the Herald’s parliament office.) Another favourite is the KFC chip, which, he says, tastes best on a late-Thursday-night sitting day. So of course we share a bowl of chips. He also selects the 200g eye fillet, and I’m quick to order the same, plus we get a side of charred sweetcorn with fermented chilli butter. Singh asks for no cheese on the corn; he’s so averse to the stuff that even the smell of melted cheese is enough to make him unwell.

Our plates are identical other than the sauce: peppercorn for Singh and mushroom for me. Our waiter recommends a 2018 Barossa Valley shiraz before I get a chance to open the wine list. I’m more of a beer drinker and am always anxious about choosing the wrong wine, so I’m relieved to leave it in our waiter’s hands. The hot chips at Chophouse. Sam Mooy Singh teams chips with eye fillet. Sam Mooy Charred sweetcorn completes the meal. Sam Mooy Singh is a “saltwater Nat”, lingo for Nationals MPs with coastal electorates, as opposed to their freshwater colleagues. His family first settled in Australia when his great-grandfather Bella Singh arrived in Cairns from Punjab in the 1890s and went to Harwood Island in the Clarence River region. Singh excitedly tells me he’s spoken with John Howard about this – his great-grandfather just happened to live in the small country town at the same time as Howard’s grandfather. I’ve seen pictures of Singh’s great-grandfather long before we meet for lunch. His photograph is one of several used by artist Peter Drew for his famous “Aussie” series, taken from documents found in the National Archives of Bella Singh’s exemption from the White Australia policy language test. Getting in contact with the artist led Singh to spend hours poring over archives, finding troves of documents, some of which he is still yet to fully examine.

Advertisement

After World War II, Bella moved to the Coffs Harbour area to work and, a century later, that’s the electorate his great-grandson represents in the NSW state parliament. Trying to win back conservative voters drawn to the anti-immigration rhetoric of One Nation without alienating the diverse members of his own electorate (Woolgoolga has a significant population of Indian heritage and is home to Australia’s first Sikh temple) will be a difficult tightrope to walk. The political fight ahead will test his leadership. Bella Singh, Gurmesh Singh’s great-grandfather, is featured on a well-known series of posters. Peter Drew Singh finds respite from the pressure of NSW politics in what sounds to me like the grimmest of situations. He’s an RFS volunteer, who enlisted after the Black Summer bushfires, but he tells me that, rather than fighting fires, most of his work has been supporting people on the worst days of their lives. Not as the boss but as the one who follows orders. “It’s not something I’ve sought to promote necessarily but plenty of people have seen me out on the fires or at car accidents and stuff, and sometimes people were a little bit surprised to see me holding a Stop/Go sign or sweeping glass off the road or rolling up a pipe or whatever it is that we’re called to do on that day. “I find it pretty rewarding. Given that I’m fairly junior in the brigade, I go there and take orders.”

One of the most confronting scenes he has responded to happened over Christmas while at a family dinner at a local beach. The brigade got a call and so Singh left the venue and headed two beaches over. A man had suffered a medical episode in the water and drowned. Paramedics were trying to resuscitate him. As an RFS volunteer his job wasn’t to be the hero but to help retrieve supplies from the ambulance as others worked to save the man’s life. “That’s often what you’re confronted with rather than actual fire, although we’ve had some hairy fires as well.” For the man with a title like NSW Nationals leader, his path to politics was fairly cosmopolitan. He attended UNSW and worked in a newsagent’s in Bondi. Straight out of university, Singh went to work for Qantas, in the marketing team, before working in software. He found a passion for politics after moving back home to farming. Singh has been at the scene of local tragedies as a member of the RFS. Sam Mooy While previous media reporting has painted Singh as a humble blueberry and macadamia farmer, that’s only part of the story. He was actually director of the powerful blueberry farmers co-op Oz Group in Woolgoolga, and was vice president of the Australian Blueberry Growers’ Association. The blueberry industry’s rapid expansion on the Mid North Coast hasn’t been without controversy, drawing concerns around pesticide use and lack of planning oversight. Dealing with land-use conflicts in horticulture and running the co-op was how Singh got interested in state politics. “Even liaising with our local council, who had a couple of Greens councillors, their solution was to add more regulation when they weren’t satisfied the existing regulation were being followed.

title: Living at home in your 20s used to be taboo. Now it’s a financial lifeline
text:

MoneySavingBudgeting Living at home in your 20s used to be taboo. Now it’s a financial lifeline Nina Hendy July 28, 2026 — 11:23am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Living at home with her parents well into her 20s has resulted in a huge financial saving that has helped 25-year-old Chloe Henry get ahead in life and also helped the communications professional save for her first overseas holiday. Henry doesn’t pay any rent to her parents, instead contributing by buying some groceries and helping with the housework. Other than that, her income is hers to do with as she pleases. Communications professional Chloe Henry says she hopes to take her parents on a holiday to thank them for letting her live at home. “I’m lucky that my parents have allowed me to stay at home for as long as I want and that they’re happy to have me there. I’m off to Japan in September for my birthday, and I can’t wait,” she says. Each morning, she travels via public transport from Berwick into Melbourne, a journey that takes 90 minutes each way. But the sacrifice has been worth it, enabling her savings to quietly grow.

Advertisement

“Living at home means I’m not feeling like I’m under a price crunch. I have a savings goal in mind, and I’ve been able to reach that goal a lot faster,” she says. But the future of life on her own isn’t entirely clear. The hope is that one day, she could be in a strong enough position to be able to rent with her partner, who is still in university. “I’m pretty pessimistic about the housing market and being able to save up to move out or put a deposit on a home. A lot of my friends still live at home and don’t have plans to move out anytime soon either.” Staying put Henry is not alone. New research from AMP shows that for many, support is no longer just about the bank of mum and dad, it’s also about the house of mum and dad, with extended families open to sharing housing, costs and care in more practical ways.

Advertisement

The shift has been driven mostly by younger singles as housing affordability, rate increases and cost of living pressures combine to make living alone increasingly unaffordable. Editor's pick Opinion

Housing affordability A new type of class divide is emerging – and property is to blame Victoria Devine Money columnist The growing number of shared living arrangements is in direct response to the constant rise in living costs, which shows no sign of easing. While common in some cultures, multi-generational living isn’t the norm in Australia. But what started during the pandemic as a way to save money as housing costs bolted has now become a way of life for many. At a time when so many people are seeking financial stability, it’s understandable that living with a flatmate could be undesirable for some given that factors outside their control – such as job losses or a large unexpected bill – could impact on their ability to cover rent.

Advertisement

Generational shift Ben Hillier, general manager of retirement solutions at AMP. Natalie Boog AMP’s research found that 68 per cent of 20- to 39-year-olds support multi-generational living, but fewer than two in five people aged 65 and over do. This points to a generational shift in expectations around independence and home ownership. “As housing pressures intensify and Australia becomes increasingly multicultural, younger Australians are rethinking what the ‘Australian dream’ looks like,” explains Ben Hillier, AMP’s director of retirement. “This shift also tells us something important about confidence for retirement, which in Australia has long been tied to home ownership. Alongside super, Australians’ sense of financial security will increasingly be shaped by the household around them – how families live, what support they can provide one another and how costs and care are shared.”

Advertisement

Mortgage brokers have noticed the change in property demand too as they’re asked to help families find homes that will accommodate extended family members, says Rebecca Jarrett-Dalton of Two Red Shoes. “Our job as brokers is no longer just about securing a rate – it’s about providing creative pathways, whether it’s navigating generational wealth when buying property, or helping families explore shared ownership,” she says. As for Henry, she admits she doesn’t have all the answers about housing in the future, but does hope that one day she can thank her parents for letting her stay home well into her 20s. “Maybe I can pay for them to take a holiday one day,” she says. title: Origin apologises after revealing 900,000 customers affected by data breach
text:
In Brief Origin says 900,000 customers were affected by a data breach.

It's advising customers to be wary of a heightened risk of scammers.

Almost one million Origin Energy customers had their details accessed by hackers after a major data breach last week, the company has revealed.

On Tuesday, Origin said it had completed an initial review into the incident and identified that approximately 900,000 current and former customers' data was accessed by the hackers.

"To our customers, I am sorry. We don't take for granted the trust customers place in Origin and our safeguarding of their information," CEO Frank Calabria said in a statement.

Last week, the energy company announced it was the victim of the security incident, saying names, addresses, dates of birth, phone numbers and account information could all have been viewed.

Other potential details include the last four digits of credit cards, or the last three digits of bank accounts.

The company said it would be contacting affected customers first and was opening up a dedicated hotline for those concerned.

Origin said it had been trying to confirm the credibility of the threat since early July.

"We worked to confirm its credibility and potential impact; however, based on the information available, it was not assessed to be credible," Calabria said.

READ MORE Origin Energy reports customer bank, credit card details caught up in data breach

"On 22 July, new information emerged that indicated a potential security incident may have occurred. We acted immediately, providing updates to the market and notifying our customers as a precaution."

Origin, which has 4.8 million customer accounts in Australia and provides electricity, natural gas, LPG and internet services, said last week it did not believe the data obtained included credit card or bank details.

Customers advised to be wary of scams

The company has also warned customers to be alert to a greater risk of scams that could arise from the data breach, advising customers to be wary of unexpected calls, emails or texts referring to their account.

Those who get such contact should independently contact Origin through numbers on official channels, it said, and do not provide passwords or personal information to anyone.

"We are acutely aware that others may exploit this incident, including by impersonating Origin or through other scam activity," Calabria said.

"We recommend that all our customers remain vigilant to suspicious activity and a heightened risk of scams.

Griffith University's Graeme Hughes, an expert on business and consumer issues, said the breach was unlikely to cause cases of payment fraud but marked a "social engineering problem".

"The last four digits for a card, a date of birth, and an authentic billing history are the exact trust signals a business uses to verify itself over the phone," Hughes told the Australian Associated Press.

"That makes an unsolicited call about an energy account far more convincing than it should be.

— With additional reporting by the Australian Associated Press.

title: Iran claims control of the Strait of Hormuz and rejects peace talks
text:
IN BRIEF Trump ended a two-week bombing campaign against Iran after advice they were running out of targets.

Iran has rejected peace talks as the US struggles to break the nation's control of the strait.

Iran says it is still in control of the Strait of Hormuz and not ‌seeking to resume peace talks with the United States.

Following 13 successive nights of intensifying bombing that provoked Iran to fire ‌on US bases in response, Trump halted the campaign over the weekend.

Iran said it would pause its own attacks for as long as the US pause in bombing endures.

Trump's decision to suspend the campaign reflected advice from his top brass ‌that the bombing, aimed at breaking Iran's grip on the strait, had reached the limits of what it could achieve, according to a US official and widespread US media reports.

The US official told Reuters that military commanders had advised the president they were running out of targets.

The official said the chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, General Dan Caine, had also expressed concern over the depletion of air defence weapons used to protect US bases in the region.

Similar reports indicating that civilian and military aides had advised Trump to halt the campaign were carried over the weekend by the New York Times, CNN, Axios and other news outlets.

The US ambassador to the United Nations, Mike Waltz, said on ‌Sunday Trump had paused ‌the campaign to allow room for negotiations.

But ⁠the spokesperson for Iran's Foreign Ministry, Esmail Baghaei, said in a televised press conference on Monday that Iran had not asked to resume peace talks with the United States.

The end of the US bombing campaign sent oil prices tumbling in the hope that disrupted global supplies could resume flowing.

Brent crude, which had briefly ticked above AU$150 a barrel last week for the first time since May, fell around 7.8 per cent by mid-morning on Monday to just under AU$130.

But in a clear bid to signal that the US bombing had failed in its objective, Tehran indicated it was still in control of the world's most important waterway for energy markets.

Several Iranian state media outlets carried the same report, citing an "informed source" as saying that Iran had turned around six "offending ships" on Monday morning that had attempted to cross the strait without ⁠its permission.

READ MORE Israeli settlers torch two mosques in West Bank during a deadly surge in violence

"As previously announced, the traffic route in the Strait ‌of Hormuz is the route specified by Iran, and other routes are contaminated and have no way out," the Iranian state media reports quoted the source as saying.

Trump launched his renewed bombing campaign to punish Iran after Tehran fired on ships using a route through the strait that ‌has been promoted by the United States, which has told vessels to sail close to the coast of Oman.

Iran says ships may pass only through a channel that runs closer to its own coast, which it controls and where it intends to impose transit fees.

The two weeks of renewed US bombing killed scores of people in Iran and destroyed bridges and tunnels across the south as well as military targets.

Four US service members were killed by Iran's return fire against US bases in neighbouring Arab states. Iran also struck civilian infrastructure in Gulf countries in what it said was retaliation for US strikes on civilian targets.

The ‌halt to the renewed US bombing campaign leaves no clear indication of what leverage the US can exert to achieve Trump's aim to break Iran's grip on the strait.

The US and Iran reached an agreement in June on a framework for talks meant to take place by the end of August to resolve major issues such as Iran's nuclear program.

READ MORE US and Iran halt bombing for second night as both sides give space to talks

But the sides have disputed the meaning of the memorandum's language about the Strait of Hormuz, with the US insisting it requires Iran to allow free travel while Iran says it grants it the authority to supervise transit.

Iran aims to formalise its control over the strait by reaching an agreement with Oman, which controls the opposite shore. A senior Omani delegation was in Tehran over the weekend discussing the future of the strait.

The foreign ministers of Qatar, the United Arab Emirates and Saudi Arabia each had held phone calls to discuss the strait with Oman's Foreign Minister Badr Albusaidi, according to reports on Monday on Qatari, UAE and Saudi state ⁠media.

Israel's Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who launched the war in February alongside Trump but has not participated in the US-Iranian negotiations to end it, is due to meet Trump in Washington early this week.

title: The green light is on for tax returns. One thing won't get your refund faster
text:
IN BRIEF The ATO has loaded a vast amount of data into its systems to make lodging tax returns easier and more accurate.

The ATO uses data matching to detect incorrect claims and may delay refunds while suspicious returns are checked.

The Australian Taxation Office (ATO) says taxpayers with straightforward tax affairs can now begin lodging their tax returns, with most income statements and pre-fill information now available.

More than 100 million pieces of data from employers, banks, private health insurers, share registries and government agencies have been loaded into the ATO's systems to help people lodge more accurately and with less effort.

ATO assistant commissioner Anita Challen released a statement saying that most income statements and pre-fill information is now available.

"If you're self-lodging, before you hit submit, take a few extra minutes to check your details to avoid delays and mistakes," she said.

The ATO is also expanding its pre-fill services this year to include income reported through the Taxable Payment Annual Report.

From late August, contractors in some industries — including construction, cleaning, courier services, information technology, road freight and security — may see that income automatically added to their returns.

Do I have 'straightforward' tax affairs?

Your tax affairs are likely to be straightforward if you're primarily paying tax on salary and wages, with only a small amount of taxable investment income or government payments.

If you're applying for more than basic deductions, or your return includes elements like capital gains, receipt of rental payments and foreign income, your return may not be straightforward.

If you're unsure, you should consult a tax accountant or services such as the ATO's Tax Help or National Tax Clinic for advice.

Common mistakes taxpayers should avoid

The ATO is also warning Australians against overclaiming deductions or failing to declare all sources of income.

That includes earnings from side hustles, cash jobs, rental properties and online content creation.

The agency says it uses sophisticated data-matching systems to detect suspicious claims and may delay refunds while returns are investigated.

Taxpayers are also being urged not to simply copy deductions from previous years if their work or circumstances have changed.

The ATO is reminding Australians that the proposed $1,000 standard work-related deduction does not apply this tax time and cannot be claimed until the 2027 tax year.

It is also warning people not to rely on tax advice from artificial intelligence platforms, social media "finfluencers", family or friends without checking official guidance or speaking to a registered tax professional.

Before lodging, the ATO recommends taxpayers check their personal details, bank account and superannuation information are up to date and ensure all pre-filled information is accurate.

READ MORE See the full list: The biggest Australian companies paying the least tax

It also encourages people to keep records of deductions, use the ATO app to track their return and remain alert to scams.

The tax office says it will never send unsolicited messages containing links asking people to log in or provide personal information.

Most tax returns are processed within 12 business days, according to the ATO, which says calling the agency will not speed up the process.

People lodging their own tax return have until 31 October, while those using a registered tax agent may have longer, provided they are on their agent's books before that date.

title: Australia's favourite holiday destination is undergoing a hidden transformation
text:
Since Bali's main landfill site, Suwung, closed in April, bags of rubbish and single-use plastics have piled up in the streets, on the beaches and in the canals.

The rest is burned.

"The air is no longer fresh; the views are clouded by haze; and the sweet scent of frangipani has been replaced by the acrid smell of burning plastic," Balinese writer Sugi Lanus posted on social media.

In June the Balinese government partially reopened the landfill to organic waste, limited to two days a week. Officials had wanted to close it for years, as the central Indonesian government pushes to end open-air waste dumping.

At the same time, tourism to Bali has hit an all-time peak. Last year, visitors increased by nearly 10 per cent to hit just under seven million visitors.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

Australians made up 1.6 million of those, according to the government's statistics bureau.

But as Indonesia paves the way for more tourists, with a master plan to transform Bali into the "Dubai" of Southeast Asia, it's the local communities who are left to shoulder the burden of Bali's environmental emergency.

Waste is a 'political issue'

Made Suarnatha, who started environmental NGO Wisnu Foundation in Bali in 1993, told SBS News Bali's waste crisis was "a political issue".

He said the landfill closure masked an existing problem with the transition from mostly organic waste to plastic waste — a problem intensified by tourism.

"You come here as a tourist, you need food, you need water, you make trips here and there, so you bring waste as a consequence," he said.

The closure of Bali's main landfill site in April made the island's waste crisis more visible. Source: Supplied / Gde Sugiarta/Wisnu Foundation

"It's no big issue when we talk about waste which is mostly organic, but the tourism industry comes, and the character of the waste changes to packaging with plastic, cardboard, metal, and everything," he said.

"It changed its character without being followed by an understanding of how to handle it."

Putu Natih, an economist at Universitas Indonesia, grew up visiting family in Bali.

She told SBS News that of the roughly 3,436 tonnes of waste generated every day in Bali, around 40 per cent is burned or illegally dumped.

"The failure is more likely structural rather than behavioural. The regulation exists, but the collection and processing infrastructure to back it up does not," Natih said.

On 12 July, environmental group Wahli Bali and student activists Frontier Bali staged a protest in the Bali capital Denpasar calling for a moratorium on tourism until the waste crisis had been addressed, also campaigning against what they see as water and land-use crises.

Source: SBS News

However, with visitors to Bali making up 45 per cent of Indonesia's overall tourism in 2025, the government is instead looking for ways to boost foreign investment in the island.

The new Dubai?

In April, the Indonesian government opened a new Kawasan Ekonomi Khusus or 'KEK', on a 498-hectare island joined to Bali by a causeway. It's called Kura Kura, or Turtle Island.

The KEK is a special economic zone offering 20-year tax holidays to foreign investors, luring them with luxury residential and shopping developments similar to the Dubai International Financial Centre.

"We will make it in a way that our financial centre is on Dubai's calibre," Indonesia's coordinating minister for economic affairs Airlangga Hartarto told reporters in June, as quoted in the Jakarta Globe.

Several facilities have already opened on the island, including a high-end shopping centre with a rooftop pool.

Natih said if the KEK had strong safeguards, like anti-money laundering oversight and rules against profit-shifting, it could be an opportunity for genuine economic development.

"I would be careful about calling it a tax haven," Natih said.

"Ultimately, the goal should be to attract businesses that can create real value, employment and innovation in Bali, not simply capital seeking lower taxes."

According to Natih, foreign investment in Bali in 2025 already sat at around 25.6 trillion rupees, or $379.39 billion.

"Foreign investment has become a major driver of Bali's economy," she said.

"The important question is not how much investment Bali receives, but what kind?" Natih said.

"Unless investors contribute to infrastructure needs to support growth, local communities end up carrying many of the environmental and social costs," Natih said.

Natih on a recent research trip to North Bali to speak to locals about waste. Source: Supplied

"Development should strengthen the relationship between people, culture and nature, not weaken it."

'Jakarta policy'

Bali has the lowest rate of unemployment in Indonesia, according to the government's Badan Pusat Statistik.

In August 2025, the unemployment rate sat at 1.49 per cent, compared to the national average of 4.85 per cent.

While foreign investment brings more jobs, the local Balinese are in "tight competition" with job seekers from other islands or foreigners.

READ MORE The awkward new rules about to kick in for travellers to Bali

Suarnatha said the spoils of the tourism industry aren't evenly distributed across the island.

"Not all foreigners coming to Bali is a tourist now, they are also seeking for jobs, and they'll create their own jobs here in Bali."

Suarnatha criticised what he called "Jakarta policy", centralised decision-making about Bali in which the community had little say.

"We rely on Jakarta...whatever decisions from Jakarta structurally, the regulation influence a lot of issues."

"It's confusing, there's no power to say 'no', and then investment goes up."

However, Suarnatha said there are positive ways for tourists to contribute to the island's sustainability.

"Actually tourists can put pressure...the Australian government can share the pressure onto the Bali government or Indonesian government," Suarnatha said.

He also called on visitors to be aware, and to spread awareness of the challenges Bali faces.

"I love my island, but my island its also feeling sad."

title: 2026 Census: Who must complete it and is it compulsory?
text:
IN BRIEF The 2026 Census is compulsory for everyone in Australia on Tuesday 11 August.

The questionnaire is in English but translators and interpreters are available for non-English speakers.

The Census is run by the Australian government every five years — but Peter Doukas, chair of the Federation of Ethnic Communities' Councils of Australia (FECCA), believes it's important to remember this questionnaire is strictly "apolitical".

Since 1911, the Australian Bureau of Statistics (ABS) has conducted the Census of Population and Housing, regardless of the political party in power. Data collected is used to inform decisions around the funding and location of schools, transport and health care services.

Doukas told SBS News the Census also provides valuable information on the demographic makeup of multicultural communities.

"It's not [about] taking a political side ... it's also not allowing the cynicism of government to get in the way of the important role that the ABS holds in collecting ... accurate demographic data about what makes up Australia," he said.

This year, the Census will be held on Tuesday 11 August. The last Census was on 10 August 2021.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

Is the Census compulsory?

The Census must be completed by every person in Australia on Census night. That includes visitors to the country, regardless of how long they have been in Australia or how long they plan to stay.

Generally, one person per household fills out the form.

People will soon receive a letter directing them to complete the Census online. Paper forms can also be requested if preferred. Credit: ABS

International visitors staying in hotels, motels, or other holiday accommodation can access paper Census forms. People staying in short-term rental accommodation (like an Airbnb or Stayz) can complete the Census online with internet access.

Do temporary visa holders need to complete the Census?

Migrants, refugees and people on temporary visas (including international students and tourists) must also complete the Census.

Doukas said people are "not giving away private information" that could be "used against them" by participating in the survey.

Confidential information, such as names and addresses, cannot be accessed by police or immigration agents.

The Census aims to capture everyone in Australia at a particular point in time, like a family photograph of the nation. Source: AAP / Jane Dempster

Online information about the Census is also available in 26 different languages via the ABS website. However, the questionnaire must be completed in English.

People who speak a language other than English can contact the Translating and Interpreting Service (TIS National) which provides access to interpreters who speak more than 150 languages.

People staying in remote and regional Australia, including fly-in fly-out workers, are expected to complete the Census.

Around 30,000 ABS field staff have been employed to ensure all Australians, including people experiencing homelessness or in hospital, can access the form. Field staff will also gather Census information from people in police custody on 11 August.

The ABS confirmed to SBS News that they receive administrative data for people in detention centres and correctional facilities within Australia which provides necessary Census details.

What happens if you provide false information?

The Census asks up to 66 questions, including an individual's gender identity, ancestry and religious affiliation.

When asked about religion during the first-ever Census in 1911, 32 people identified as "Wowser" and 21 as "Angelic". In the 2011 Census, more than 64,000 people in Australia marked their religion as "Jedi".

The ABS maintains "every response matters" during the Census and helps determine the distribution of public funds. Providing false or misleading statements or information is considered an offence and can result in a fine of up to $3,640.

He would not say whether these "announcements" related to fuel supply or storage, saying Australians would have to wait for the details.

title: Why your hairdresser might not know how to cut your curls
text:
This audio is voiced by AI and may occasionally mispronounce words.

Veronica Vazquez has always had curly hair, but she hasn't always embraced it.

Growing up in the countryside, she says her curls made her stand out.

"Everyone had straight blonde hair. I remember going to school, getting water from the bubbler and flattening all my hair down because it was just too much," she tells SBS News.

Inheriting her curls from her Spanish father, Vazquez says her mother, who is of Malaysian heritage, didn't have the tools or knowledge to style and manage curly hair.

Now a mother herself, she has watched her nine-year-old daughter, Ivory, who also has curly hair, face the same challenges of standing out among her peers at school.

She says she's determined to break the cycle and empower her daughter to feel confident about her appearance.

Veronica Vazquez is determined to give her daughter the confidence to embrace her curly hair, something she says took her years to learn herself. Source: SBS News

"I just have to embrace, educate and show her all the beautiful styles that are possible with curly hair."

For many Australians with curly, coily and afro-textured hair, finding a hairdresser with the right skills remains a challenge. Stylists say the problem starts in the classroom, where training has long failed to keep pace with the needs of textured hair.

Finding a stylist who understands curls

A horror haircut is a common experience within the curly hair community.

Unlike straight hair, curly, coily, afro or textured hair has a different structure that requires specialised cutting techniques. Experienced stylists often cut textured hair while it is dry to better understand how the curls fall and frame the face.

Vazquez and her daughter travel nearly two hours to Curl Lab in Sydney, a salon specialising in curly hair cuts and education, but she says it took years of trial and error to find the right place.

"We went to one salon, and they straightened Ivory's hair and cut it. Unfortunately, her hair is never straight, so by the time we've gone home, showered, the curls bounced up and it was just chopped everywhere," she says.

It's really no fault of the stylist; they're just not educated in how to cut curly hair.

Curl Lab owner Natasha Thandekafountas says the current hair education system teaches students the same cutting techniques for clients with both straight and textured or afro hair, rather than providing training tailored to different hair types.

"If you're cutting curly hair when it's straightened or wet, it's going to look good until the curls bounce up," Thandekafountas tells SBS News.

Sydney-based salon owner Natasha Thandekafountas says the current hair education system fails to tailor cutting techniques to different hair types. Source: SBS News

"We like to call it the 'Lord Farquaad' bob, so many clients come in for us to fix that," referring to the character from the film Shrek, who has a pageboy bob haircut.

How history shaped hair standards

The challenges faced by many people with curly and afro-textured hair are rooted in decades of beauty standards that experts say favoured straight hair.

Early anthropologists and naturalists once used the colour and texture of hair as markers of social hierarchy.

Farida Fozdar, a sociologist and professor of anthropology at Curtin University, says hair texture, much like race, was historically used to reinforce ideas about status, with so-called 'Caucasian hair' — blonde, light coloured or straight hair — often viewed as the ideal.

"There was a bit of a tendency to assume kinky, or curly hair was somehow abnormal or a lesser quality of hair," she tells SBS News.

"There were a number of researchers who described it as 'woolly' hair, suggesting it was more like animals."

Fozdar says those attitudes began to shift as Australia became more culturally diverse following the end of the White Australia policy and the increase in migration from the 1960s onwards.

"People who migrated in the 60s, 70s and 80s found it very difficult to find hair salons, but there is a growing awareness about the need to cater to populations who are different," she says.

While specialist salons are now becoming more common, many stylists say education and training have struggled to keep pace with Australia's diverse population.

Why hairdressing education is falling short

More than a decade ago, afro and curly hair education became part of the national training curriculum developed by Service and Creative Skills Australia (SaCSA), the Jobs and Skills Council for personal services.

However, the content is delivered as optional training in some qualifications, meaning many apprentice hairdressers can complete their studies with little or no practical experience working with textured hair.

In some states, including NSW, there's an elective unit on using a protein treatment to relax curly hair that teaches professionals to analyse hair, select products, apply heat, and smooth curls.

Amelia Canet, a curl stylist based in Sydney, says the standard hairdressing training qualification doesn't adequately cover the basics.

Many hair stylists say hairdressing and barbering training has struggled to keep pace with Australia's diverse population. Source: SBS News

"There wasn't any curl education at all. If we did have any textured clients, we were told just blow-dry them," she tells SBS News.

Other curly stylists, like Tulsi Prasad, say they had to take matters into their own hands and teach themselves to cut and style textured hair.

"I just had to learn on my own, watch my own videos, do my own private course, but go through TAFE to learn the proper ways to do everything else," she tells SBS News.

Salon owner Thandekafountas says she invests heavily in training because graduates often arrive without the skills needed to confidently work with textured hair. She sets aside a portion of the business budget to train new staff.

"We need to catch up. Close that gap and really have things mainstreamed," she says.

"How come we're not being serviced in the same way someone with straight hair is?"

It's not just hair; it's our identity, it's our culture, and for so long we've been told that it's too big, it's too busy, it's not professional. So we really want to change that image.

The push for curriculum reform

In March 2025, SaCSA began reviewing and updating its standards for some of the hairdressing and barbering qualifications to ensure they align with current industry practice and workforce needs.

Part of its proposal includes recommendations for three new units focusing on cutting and colouring curly and coily hair.

Natalie Turmine, CEO of SaCSA, says learners will also gain knowledge of the history and culture of curly and coily hair, but adds there isn't enough demand in the industry for the units to become compulsory parts of the curriculum.

"As demand and industry become more aware and more customers are coming in and that demand builds, then we'll be able to look at potentially building in skill sets and building it in as a mandatory part of the qualification," she tells SBS News.

SaCSA is undertaking a review of some hairdressing and barbering qualifications to ensure they align with current industry practice and workforce needs. Source: SBS News

For the hairdressing industry, the recommendations represent more than just new training units — they signal growing recognition of the need for textured hair education.

Fiona Beamish, CEO of the Australian Hairdressing Council, says the proposed reforms are a significant first step and hopes the units will eventually become compulsory.

"Data tells us that we are ready for this training package to include these units and I'd like to think in the future we could have this as a mandatory training package," she tells SBS News.

Driving change from within the industry

The push for better training comes as the hairdressing industry continues to grapple with a shortage of skilled workers.

According to Jobs and Skills Australia, only 45 per cent of advertised hairdressing roles were filled in 2022-23, with 85 per cent of applicants deemed unsuitable.

A 2026 SaCSA report examining the drivers behind the hairdressing workforce shortage found the sustainability issue is largely linked to "outdated course content and insufficient workforce preparation", raising broader questions about whether current training is meeting the industry's needs.

READ MORE How a hairdressing client list became a campaign to help Jay and Jeremy become dads

Sydney hairstylist and educator Chrissy Zemura has spent years delivering private courses and professional education, and creating products for customers with textured hair.

In 2020, she started an online petition calling for a mandatory module on curly and afro-textured hair, which attracted more than 42,000 signatures.

"While the curriculum is the mountain peak, a lot has changed over the past six years, including people's mindsets," Zemura tells SBS News.

SaCSA says the updated training recommendations are in the final stages of review with state and federal departments. They will then be assessed by the Assurance Body before the new training package is published early next year.

title: 'Very volatile stock': A caution to Tesla investors as Musk doubles down on AI
text:
in brief Tesla's profits have dropped after heavy investment in artificial intelligence weighed on earnings.

Some experts say companies may have to invest heavily in AI to stay competitive in the future.

Financial analysts have warned not to expect much stability in Tesla's share price after CEO Elon Musk defended billions of dollars of investment at the electric vehicle manufacturer, which has just seen one of its worst stock market falls in years.

This week, Tesla reported second-quarter profit of $US1.1 billion ($1.57 billion), down about 5 per cent from a year earlier, as lower vehicle prices and heavy investment in artificial intelligence weighed on the company's earnings.

The result translated to 33 cents a share, well below analysts' expectations of 53 cents, while revenue rose 26 per cent to $28.2 billion.

Although Tesla beat expectations for second-quarter vehicle deliveries earlier this month, the company said profitability was hit by lower vehicle selling prices, reduced revenue from regulatory credits and unspecified "energy warranty-related charges".

Capital expenditure more than doubled to $5.8 billion ($8.3 billion) during the quarter as Tesla accelerated investment in AI and manufacturing.

Tesla is embarking on a massive construction spree that Musk characterised on a conference call as probably the United States' "fastest industrial scale-up since World War Two".

The company said production of its Cybercab had begun in Texas, the Tesla Semi remained on track for 2026, and subscriptions to its Full Self-Driving driver-assistance program continued to grow.

Asked about scaling Tesla's robotaxi business, Musk said the company was focused on achieving near-perfect reliability.

"How many nines of reliability do you need to scale?" Musk said. "Ideally, you want 99.99999, you know, per cent reliable."

AI investments are 'very expensive'

Tesla's spending has drawn scrutiny from investors concerned about returns on its AI investments.

CFRA Research analyst Garrett Nelson said uncertainty over the spending had weighed on Tesla shares.

"They just haven't been very transparent with [Wall] Street on the expected return of the dollars that have been spent."

Jai Mirchandani, chief executive of Elm Responsible Investments, said the spending reflected Tesla's long-term strategy.

"The company and Musk is saying that it's one of the best investment opportunities and that's why they're investing so heavily in AI and robotics primarily," he told SBS News.

"As we've seen from companies like even Google and Microsoft and all the tech leaders, it's very expensive, and it requires a lot of capital to build the AI infrastructure and technology.

"And if you want to succeed in this space, our view is that you have to be investing in AI and innovation."

Mirchandani described AI as a revolutionary technology that needs "a lot of capital investment".

Musk defends Tesla spending

Musk said Tesla's capital expenditure (capex) was justified, saying the company "should be spending on capex as fast as we can spend ... without it being too wasteful".

"It's OK to be a little less capital efficient if we get things done sooner."

Tesla's chief financial officer Vaibhav Taneja said research and development costs would "continue to grow in 2026 and beyond".

Speculation has also grown about closer ties between Tesla and SpaceX following the rocket company's stock market debut, although Musk declined to discuss any potential combination.

READ MORE Musk becomes first trillionaire in history as SpaceX shares soar

"There's more and more overlap," said Musk.

"Obviously, we can't talk about combining companies and that kind of thing on an earnings call. It's got to be done with the appropriate process."

Mirchandani cautioned investors about Tesla's share price movements.

"The reality is that Tesla is a very volatile stock. And so I'd sort of just be mindful of that."

Watch and see

Stockbroker Richard Hemming said investors were increasingly rewarding companies that continued to innovate.

"I think the innovation part of it is more worrying for investors for companies that don't innovate," he told SBS News.

"I think that, in the next reporting season, it's going to be interesting to see how companies ... are going in the sales line. "

He said Australia's upcoming corporate reporting season would provide an important test of company profitability.

"We are seeing sort of signs, especially in Australia, that productivity's falling," he said.

"Productivity in Australia has been under a lot of pressure versus the rest of the world because I guess we're not seeing the kind of innovation that they're seeing in the US.

"So definitely, the upcoming results are going to be very, very important. "

Breaking BusinessCompaniesAdvertising Gerry Harvey branded the legal system unjust. It has come back to bite him Elias Visontay July 28, 2026 — 12:38pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A judge has singled out comments from billionaire retailer Gerry Harvey calling the legal system “f---ed” as a factor in slapping his company Harvey Norman with $35 million in penalties for running misleading ads. On Tuesday, Justice Michael O’Bryan made the orders against both Harvey Norman and credit company Latitude Finance Australia – which must pay $20 million in penalties – over a misleading and deceptive advertising campaign spruiking the latter’s credit card product. Harvey Norman chairman Gerry Harvey arriving at Lachlan Murdoch’s annual Christmas party in Sydney’s Bellevue Hill in December. Oscar Colman The Australian Securities and Investments Commission (ASIC) had taken Harvey Norman and Latitude to court over a national ad campaign that ran between January 2020 and August 2021, which promoted products as available via a “no-deposit” and 60-month interest-free payment method. But it failed to disclose that customers were actually required to sign up for a credit card with high establishment and monthly fees to access the deal. In October 2024, the Federal Court found the companies had misled people with the ads, saying customers entered a “fundamentally different financial arrangement” than the one promoted. An appeal by Harvey Norman and Latitude was dismissed in September 2025.

Advertisement

In delivering his decision on penalties, O’Bryan highlighted how Harvey Norman and Latitude responded to the case in significantly different ways. “Neither company had a suitable process for ensuring that their advertising complied with the consumer protection laws. Given the scale and sophistication of both defendants, that is an extraordinary state of affairs,” O’Bryan said. He said it was “particularly striking in the case of Harvey Norman, given the size of the company”. He added that while Latitude had since provided “evidence of the steps that it has now taken to improve its processes in that regard”, Harvey Norman failed to do so. “That is a distinguishing feature between the two defendants, relatedly, the defendants have also exhibited a different level of contrition,” O’Bryan said. “Latitude’s general counsel offered an apology to Latitude’s customers on behalf of the company.

Advertisement

Related Article Retail ‘We all get hammered’: Harvey Norman’s court battles don’t faze Gerry “In contrast, no executive or legal counsel of Harvey Norman gave evidence about the company’s compliance procedures or offered an apology, and public statements made by Harvey Norman’s chairman show a disregard for the potential harm suffered by consumers from Harvey Norman’s misleading conduct.” A month after the court’s initial 2024 decision, the retailer’s namesake, Gerry Harvey, declined to specifically discuss the case and said his lawyers did not want him talking about the topic, but he unleashed on the legal system as a whole. “If I had my way, I’d be out there screaming at the top of my lungs about the injustices, and yet I can’t do it. I’ve got to play along with it,” he told this masthead at the time. “The whole legal system is completely f---ed in Australia.” O’Bryan said that taking into account those considerations had led him to decide more significant penalties for Harvey Norman. “A higher penalty is warranted to deter repetition and to motivate Harvey Norman to improve its compliance processes,” he said.

Advertisement

Harvey, who was contacted by phone for comment on Tuesday, downplayed his involvement in the company, which is now run by his wife Katie Page as chief executive. “I used to sell fridges, but now I’m a farmer,” Harvey said. In the full judgment, O’Bryan was scathing of Harvey’s comments: “Mr Harvey is entitled to express his opinions, including about the legal system. However, Mr Harvey’s opinions indicate that the Chairman of Harvey Norman’s sole focus is upon the perceived injustice suffered by Harvey Norman, and a complete disregard for the potential harm suffered by consumers from Harvey Norman’s misleading conduct.” “Taking the evidence as a whole, I am not persuaded that Harvey Norman has demonstrated any contrition for its wrongful conduct,” O’Bryan said. O’Bryan also said that while the quantifiable harm to consumers was likely less than $5 million, consumers may have wasted their time investigating the offer, or become so invested before realising its true terms that they ultimately proceeded. As such, he estimated the incremental revenue earned by each party through the contravening conduct was about $5 million.

Advertisement

Both Harvey Norman and Latitude will also have to publish notices on their websites about the orders for 90 days, and pay ASIC’s costs. ASIC had been seeking penalties of $50 million against Harvey Norman and $35 million against Latitude, as well as injunctions restraining the companies from advertising similar deals for five years, which O’Bryan did not order. title: Tears, defiance and unspoken truths: Reading between the lines of Jacinta Allan’s farewell speech
text:
Jacinta Allan’s exit speech focused heavily on her decades of achievement, but the Commonwealth Games and Big Build corruption were glaring omissions. This feature looks past the official farewell to examine the frustration, the failures and the fault lines of her premiership.

In Glasgow, Australian athletes have dominated the 2026 Commonwealth Games medal table – a success Premier Jacinta Allan was once supposed to bask in. But their glory ended up taking place far away from her. Instead, Allan was attempting to fend off a leadership challenge from colleagues despairing at Labor’s bleak prospects of retaining power in November’s state election. The government’s disastrous, and some might say farcical, decision to withdraw as host of the games just months before Allan became leader eliminated any prospect of political gain Labor might have hoped for from the event. That decision, along with Allan’s role as minister for Commonwealth Games delivery – among her many other senior portfolios before taking the reins as premier – helped lay the groundwork for this week’s coup, which ultimately saw Victoria’s second female premier resign on Tuesday morning. In her resignation speech, Victorians saw the emotional range that Allan carried as she reflected on her legacy. Her time was up, but she insisted she was not done fighting. Through tears and smiles and trademark defiance, Allan spoke about her many achievements. She thanked her supporters, but her voice wavered when speaking of the many moments with her family she had sacrificed. “I would have absolutely relished the fight this November. I was more than ready.” Jacinta Allan, exit speech

Advertisement

There were many omissions, most importantly when it came to Big Build corruption and of course the Commonwealth Games. Girl, interrupted: Jacinta Allan arrives to relinquish the premiership. Jason South In 2022, together with then premier Daniel Andrews, Allan promised a boon for the regions where they planned to stage the games. At the time, the Andrews government’s ascendancy mirrored the Australian swimming team’s current performance – easily dominating its middling rivals at the games in Glasgow. New housing and sports venues. Jobs. Invaluable attention on the world stage. Business and cultural opportunities. The government spruiked these selling points at every opportunity. Jacinta Allan at a level crossing removal in 2016, when she was public transport minister. Eddie Jim The decision to abruptly withdraw as host invited ridicule after such grandiose promises, and the games quickly became a symbol of the political baggage the government had accumulated over three imposing terms in power. When Andrews resigned as premier in September 2023, that burden became Allan’s to carry. She never seemed to free herself from its weight.

Advertisement

In a cruel twist of fate, some of Allan’s greatest ministerial achievements added significantly to her undoing. After Labor’s return to office at the 2014 election, Allan held some of the most senior and prominent portfolios in the government, including transport and infrastructure, priority precincts, major projects and the Suburban Rail Loop. Daniel Andrews and Jacinta Allan on a tour of the new Town Hall Station, part of the Metro Tunnel project, in 2022. Nicki Connolly On Tuesday, Allan gave profuse thanks for the opportunity to see projects including the Metro Tunnel through to completion. “They are not just projects; they are assets that will improve our lives.” Jactina Allan, exit speech Her successful leadership in the level crossing removal program provided the Andrews government with a weapon they used to clobber political opponents. Andrews and Allan traversed the city to “apologise for the progress we’re making” with their infrastructure projects. They turned the inconvenience of construction works into a real-time billboard for their city-building agenda. Every disruption, train replacement bus and even compulsory property acquisitions became deftly wielded political advantages.

Advertisement

She always seemed to be at Andrews’ side during infrastructure press conferences, high-vis vests and hard hats reinforcing visually their commitment to working for Victoria. They carried away boom gates, inspected underground works on the Metro Tunnel and stood beside the routes for planned roads, while the opposition floundered in relative anonymity. These projects – as well as the West Gate Tunnel, Regional Rail Revival, Melbourne Airport Rail and North East Link – came to be known as the Big Build. “Thank you to Daniel Andrews, who taught us to put people first” Jactina Allan, exit speech But through all those media appearances, Andrews was the undeniable star of the show. Allan had a strong command of the government’s many projects and their mechanics and complexities. Yet Andrews’ authoritative presence gave little chance for his colleague to truly shine. Before her retirement from politics in 2022, some political observers had expected it would be Jill Hennessy – Allan’s factional ally from the Left – who would take over from Andrews.

Advertisement

When it came to charming the press pack on tour buses during election campaigns or explaining emotionally complex policies, including the government’s voluntary assisted dying reforms, Hennessy was a star performer. She had the kind of warm and common touch in media appearances that Allan lacked. Yet, even if Allan had been a stronger media performer, there was no way of spinning the corruption and cost overruns that plagued the projects for which she was responsible. Revelations published by The Age of organised crime inflating the cost of the government’s infrastructure agenda to the tune of billions of dollars dealt a devastating blow to Allan’s credibility. Reporting by investigative journalist Nick McKenzie that Mick Gatto was benefiting from the Big Build caught public attention in a way that few news stories can. Victorians across the state were outraged that gangland figures were profiting at the public’s expense while their roads lay riddled with tyre-popping potholes. Like the government’s handling of the botched Commonwealth Games bid, Allan had no way of claiming plausible deniability about the cost overruns and organised crime presence. It all happened on her watch. Premier Jacinta Allan has rejected multiple calls for a royal commission into corruption on the Big Build. Eddie Jim

title: We might be sitting on a $2,600,000,000,000,000 bomb
text:

BusinessThe economyGlobal economy Opinion We might be sitting on a $2,600,000,000,000,000 bomb Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist July 28, 2026 — 11:57am

July 28, 2026 — 11:57am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Global wealth is booming, but it is on increasingly shaky foundations. Last week the McKinsey Global Institute issued its annual global balance sheet. It estimated that global wealth hit almost $US1.8 quadrillion ($2.6 quadrillion, with a quadrillion equalling a thousand trillion) last year. In 2024, it was $US1.7 quadrillion. McKinsey’s annual report warned that increases in wealth are being driven by paper gains, rather than by real economic growth. AP While that might be regarded as an indicator of an increasingly prosperous world, McKinsey referred to the “mounting detachment” of the balance sheet from the global economy, with several asset classes growing further out of balance with the underlying growing economy. Essentially, it is saying that most of the increases in wealth are being driven by paper gains, rather than by real economic growth.

Advertisement

It singled out US equities, where values “soared” to 2.4 times corporate net assets, with profits double their share of GDP relative to their shares in 2000. China’s corporate debt, it said, grew to 80 per cent of real assets against a global average of 50 per cent, while government debt was near all-time highs in the US and was growing most rapidly in China. Related Article Luxury property Where Australia’s richest people live and how much it costs to live there Of the global increase in household wealth to $US570 trillion, only 20 per cent came from real capital formation – new investment in machinery and equipment, buildings, infrastructure and intellectual property – with valuations of existing assets growing 4 percentage points faster than already high consumer price inflation. It is valuations and inflation driving the balance sheet expansion, not economic growth. Macquarie Capital’s Viktor Shvets has long spoken and written about “hyper-financialisation” and “a cloud of finance” in which the growth of financial assets far outstrips, and is disconnected from, real economies.

Advertisement

He’s also written of what he calls the “Fujiwara effect” (when several hurricanes merge), or the fusion of deep financialisation with a disruptive acceleration of the Information Age. The coincidence of financialisation and technological advancement, he has argued, generates an over accumulation of capital, displacement of labour by technology, rising inequality and social tensions and intense disinflation. The largest asset class within the McKinsey balance sheet is real estate, where values (except in Australia, at least until very recently) have been correcting relative to GDP. Louie Douvis McKinsey detailed the implications of a balance sheet outrunning the underlying economy, and there are echoes of Shvets’ view of the world in its conclusions. When real estate and equity values rise faster than GDP, it says, weaknesses can be exposed, capital can flow disproportionately to asset repurchases, sometimes with a lot of leverage and while, valuations might rise, the real economy might be deprived of the investment that drives long-term growth.

Advertisement

“For households, wealth rises but merely on paper, with heightened risk of eventual corrections. Growing asset values also tend to exacerbate wealth inequality, as existing owners of wealth see large gains while entering asset markets becomes harder for others.” Related Article Opinion

Elon Musk Before we build a statue of Elon Musk, let’s consider what he’s done with his trillions of dollars Shane Wright Senior economics correspondent It nominates three ways in which an overly inflated balance sheet might correct. One, the most benign, is with productivity-driven growth in the real economy that boosts income to validate high asset valuations and high levels of debt. Artificial intelligence holds out that promise, although at present it is probably doing more to exacerbate asset values and leverage than to increase productivity and boost real income.

Advertisement

The other two options aren’t as palatable. Sustained inflation would erode the real value of assets and debt while producing higher nominal GDP while a balance sheet “reset” – a sharp drop in asset values, significant deleveraging, corporate and personal defaults, losses of wealth and employment and lower economic growth – would also shrink the balance sheet. Macquarie Capital’s Viktor Shvets has long spoken and written about “hyper-financialisation ” and “a cloud of finance” in which the growth of financial assets far outstrips, and is disconnected from, real economies. Dion Georgopoulos That’s what happened when the dot-com bubble burst in 2000, and when the global financial crisis occurred in 2008. An abrupt shrinking of the global balance sheet to realign it with the underlying global economy would, as it was in those past instances, be traumatic. The world could, of course, just muddle along with the kind of stagnation that developed during the period after the 2008 global financial crisis, with low growth, low interest rates, low investment and increasing leverage, although it is hard to see how that could be a sustainable condition.

Advertisement

A breakdown of trends within the McKinsey balance sheet shows equity is now 2.8 times global GDP, against an average of 1.9 times over the preceding 24 years since 2000. Government debt, at 0.9 per cent of GDP, has edged up from 0.8 times and corporate debt has done the same. Household debt has edged down from 0.8 to 0.7 times, while currency and deposits have risen from 1.5 times GDP to 1.7 times. “Growing asset values also tend to exacerbate wealth inequality, as existing owners of wealth see large gains while entering asset markets becomes harder for others.” McKinsey report The largest asset class within the balance sheet is real estate, where values (except in Australia, at least until very recently) have been correcting relative to GDP, and the second-largest is equity, where values relative to GDP are at all-time highs in some countries.

Advertisement

That’s most notably the case in the US, which accounts for nearly half of the total of global equity and where equity values are 2.4 times net assets. In most other countries they are around 1 times net assets. The other big element in the balance sheet is debt, where household debt has been trending down, but corporate debt in China has nearly doubled the global average, and government debt – relative to GDP – had the fastest growth. Government debt was above 100 per cent of GDP in Japan, the US, Italy, France, Canada, Belgium, Spain and the UK. Government debt was near all-time highs in the US and was growing most rapidly in China. Bloomberg In the US, massive deficits, debt levels that are swelling inexorably, inflation and rising bond yields are raising threat levels while in other parts of the world unbalanced or weak growth, when combined with high levels of government debt, also threaten. The world’s two key economies – the US and China – face different challenges. The US needs to consume less and save more, while China needs to save less and consume more (and perhaps invest more productively).

Advertisement

Related Article Opinion

Trade wars Trump’s America is sinking as his war on the world sputters Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist The best-case scenario is for artificial intelligence to deliver, benignly, on its promise of a leap change in productivity, although how those benefits, if they do emerge, are shared will have profound social implications. The world doesn’t need – and probably wouldn’t tolerate – the wealth from those productivity gains being captured by a handful of trillionaires. It remains plausible, however, that an AI sector that is still in a development phase and built on access to equity at ever-inflating valuations and access to ever-increasing amounts of cheap debt won’t reach a level of maturity, with positive cashflows and maybe even actual earnings, before investors run out of patience or capacity to support it. That’s the year-2000 scenario, which would be a setback, albeit not necessarily a permanent one, for a productivity-led resetting/rescue of a global balance sheet that, on McKinsey’s analysis, appears vulnerable and, perhaps, unsustainable. Lo Presti’s is an “unassumingly delicious” new restaurant overlooking Redfern Park, opened by former Baba’s Place head chef Michael Lo Presti and restaurant manager Rachael Trewin. “It’s not going to look flashy, but there’s going to be a lot of care in what we do,” said Lo Presti, of the Mediterranean-leaning menu featuring grilled pork with local pipis, ling wrapped in vine leaves, and an avgolemono sour cocktail, inspired by the Greek lemon chicken soup. 1 / 7 Owners Rachael Trewin and chef Michael Lo Presti. It’s a two-storey corner terrace, with one of Lo Presti’s father Greg’s old sketches repurposed into an illuminated sign out front. Opening a restaurant of his own was always part of the plan, Lo Presti said. He grew up in the family’s Darlinghurst restaurant of the same name and watched as regulars became friends.

Lo Presti went on to three-hatted Stanmore restaurant Sixpenny, and was a finalist in The Sydney Morning Herald Good Food Guide 2024 Young Chef of the Year award. Their friendship endured, and for the past two years they worked alongside each other at hatted Marrickville restaurant Baba’s Place. They’d always talked about wanting to open a place of their own, somewhere they’d want to go for dinner themselves, said Lo Presti. It made sense to do it together.

“I went on holiday down to Melbourne and Tasmania and I saw all these small, independently run restaurants and I’m like … I think it’s time, now, to do it myself,” he said. “It’s getting harder and harder these days to open up an independent restaurant and we thought we’d just get our foot in the door.” Lo Presti’s is designed to make diners feel like “you’re coming over to someone’s house for a dinner party”. Dion Georgopoulos The goal was to create a warm, inviting space where diners could just as well walk in for a glass of Montepulciano at the bar, or book ahead for a relaxed Sunday lunch on the terrace. “I want it to feel like you’re coming over to someone’s house for a dinner party, but it’s actually a functioning restaurant,” Trewin said.

The menu is deliberately understated. A plate of roasted capsicum is dehydrated, just slightly (“so it’s a little bit chewier and the flavours are fortified”), and dressed simply with Pedro Ximenez vinegar. Braised kangaroo tail, swaps oxtail for “such an underutilised cut”, marinated overnight in an “almost-Caribbean style” spice blend, then braised until it’s “sticky, rich and dark”, served with salsa. Hanger steak. Dion Georgopoulos “It’s rich, but there’s respite in that dish with salsa and fresh mint,” Lo Presti said. The wine list stays predominantly local, offering a range of price points, with a rotating option imported from Europe.

“We want it to be a warm, comfortable place … but fun, a little bit loud, with a lot of regulars … you know, you come in, you sit in the same spot, we know what you like,” Lo Presti said. “I think it will be the kind of place where people come in and feel like they’re contributing something to the restaurant, like they’re part of something, because customers really do contribute.” Open lunch Sat-Sun; dinner Thu-Sat Level 1, 34b Redfern Street, Redfern (entrance via Elizabeth Street), loprestisrestaurant.com

Washington: If you’re feeling a touch sorry for yourself, Alex De Minaur can recommend a cure - get married. The 27-year-old from Sydney wedded fellow tennis star Katie Boulter just after Wimbledon, a tournament he exited in a disappointing round of 16 loss to Italy’s Flavio Cobolli. By his own admission, De Minaur was beating himself up. Alex de Minaur on his wedding day. Kate Julia “It breaks me inside. That’s the reality of it,” he said at the time. “Many, many hours get put into my craft, and countless years, to have moments like these. To not step up to the plate is truly gut-wrenching.” But the wedding - first an intimate ceremony in England, then a larger celebration in Tuscany, and a very brief honeymoon in Portofino - has helped cast those blues aside, and recharge the batteries.

Advertisement

“We did the maths, it’s probably the longest I’ve ever had without touching a racquet,” he says on the sidelines of the Mubadala DC Open in Washington. “It was probably about 13 days.” Thirteen days is a veritable eternity in the hectic schedule of professional tennis, which De Minaur thinks should be shortened. On Sunday, he talked about needing a break around this time of year, after the Roland Garros-Wimbledon double act and before the lead-up to the US Open. Alex de Minaur and Katie Boulter on their wedding day. Kate Julia De Minaur doesn’t regret baring his soul in the aftermath of his Wimbledon defeat, but he feels it was overblown. His raw post-match news conference, in which he seemed on the verge of tears, received a lot of attention. “I don’t think it was warranted, as much as - myself included - a lot of people wanted to make a big deal out of it,” he says now.

“It became a really big thing, but realistically it took me a couple of days to get over it. It was just the same feelings and emotions that any athlete has after a tough loss. His challenge is to channel that success into mental resilience on court – as he says, to play more freely and “with a little bit less weight on my shoulders”. The burden of expectation is heavy these days. Does he feel pressure to win from the Australian tennis public? “It mainly comes from myself,” he says. “As you win more matches, as you get closer to the top, more and more people have opinions on you than they did 10 years ago … It just comes with the job. “In fact, it’s a good thing. I’ve earned the right for people to have opinions about myself and my tennis.
