If opposition leader is the most unenviable job in politics, then Nationals leader in opposition has to be a close second. Gurmesh Singh, a Coffs Harbour macadamia and blueberry farmer-turned-politician, was elevated to that position in November last year. Along with Liberal leader Kellie Sloane, who gained office only days later, he became a newly minted political leader just weeks before the country’s worst-ever terror attack. Now he’s the man tasked with saving his party’s regional NSW seats from a One Nation avalanche at next year’s election. He’s also the first Sikh elected to an Australian parliament and the first Sikh leader of a major party. He has a rich family history, and a portrait of Singh’s great-grandfather is plastered on walls around the country. When we sit down to lunch on a rainy Sydney Tuesday, One Nation has been surging in the polls, and most of the talk on Macquarie Street about the Nationals often concludes with something like “they’re in major trouble”. I know it’s probably not what Singh wants me to talk about but I can’t help but ask how he feels about Pauline Hanson’s surge in popularity and her calls for a monoculture, given his own background. “I grew up in the ’80s and ’90s in what we would describe as Australian culture, in what some of these people are saying they’d like us to be,” he says. “It’s a good culture that I would also like to live in again. “I look at myself [and my family] – we’ve got a different ethnicity, obviously we have different religious beliefs, and we might have slightly different festivals and religious celebrations, but I think you can do that while still being uniquely Australian as well, and I think that’s the more mature conversation that we should be having … how do we – and you can – do both.”

Advertisement

“I think what people are actually looking for is what we had back then. That’s safer streets, that was an economy that meant you could have a house with one income, it meant kids who were out on their bikes, meant you could go to the beach on a weekend – like, these are the things that people remember … It’s actually things that government should be striving for, right?” The most recent Resolve Political Monitor conducted over June and July found support for the Coalition at the lowest in recent memory, down to 23 per cent and trailing behind One Nation, which sat at 25 per cent despite not yet having a single endorsed candidate for the NSW election. Singh says he believes the tides will turn in the time between now and the March poll, and that Coalition policies like a reduction in payroll tax, released earlier than usual in this election cycle, will get people back on board with the core Nationals principles of smaller governments and better infrastructure for the bush. Related Article Editorial

Resolve Political Monitor NSW voters revolt against major parties The Herald's View Editorial We’re lunching at Matt Moran’s Chophouse in Sydney’s CBD, a sophisticated steak house a short walk from Parliament House where Singh is familiar with the menu. He has a secret passion for hot chips, a love so deep that in his younger years he tried his hand at building an online map of his best reviewed offerings in Sydney. The chips at Chophouse and Bondi’s Hotel Ravesis are up there among the best, he says, but so are those from parliament’s Long Bell Cafe. (I share this enthusiasm and am all too familiar with the salty, crunchy goodness, given the kitchen is mere steps from the Herald’s parliament office.) Another favourite is the KFC chip, which, he says, tastes best on a late-Thursday-night sitting day. So of course we share a bowl of chips. He also selects the 200g eye fillet, and I’m quick to order the same, plus we get a side of charred sweetcorn with fermented chilli butter. Singh asks for no cheese on the corn; he’s so averse to the stuff that even the smell of melted cheese is enough to make him unwell.

Advertisement

Our plates are identical other than the sauce: peppercorn for Singh and mushroom for me. Our waiter recommends a 2018 Barossa Valley shiraz before I get a chance to open the wine list. I’m more of a beer drinker and am always anxious about choosing the wrong wine, so I’m relieved to leave it in our waiter’s hands. The hot chips at Chophouse. Sam Mooy Singh teams chips with eye fillet. Sam Mooy Charred sweetcorn completes the meal. Sam Mooy Singh is a “saltwater Nat”, lingo for Nationals MPs with coastal electorates, as opposed to their freshwater colleagues. His family first settled in Australia when his great-grandfather Bella Singh arrived in Cairns from Punjab in the 1890s and went to Harwood Island in the Clarence River region. Singh excitedly tells me he’s spoken with John Howard about this – his great-grandfather just happened to live in the small country town at the same time as Howard’s grandfather. I’ve seen pictures of Singh’s great-grandfather long before we meet for lunch. His photograph is one of several used by artist Peter Drew for his famous “Aussie” series, taken from documents found in the National Archives of Bella Singh’s exemption from the White Australia policy language test. Getting in contact with the artist led Singh to spend hours poring over archives, finding troves of documents, some of which he is still yet to fully examine.

Advertisement

After World War II, Bella moved to the Coffs Harbour area to work and, a century later, that’s the electorate his great-grandson represents in the NSW state parliament. Trying to win back conservative voters drawn to the anti-immigration rhetoric of One Nation without alienating the diverse members of his own electorate (Woolgoolga has a significant population of Indian heritage and is home to Australia’s first Sikh temple) will be a difficult tightrope to walk. The political fight ahead will test his leadership. Bella Singh, Gurmesh Singh’s great-grandfather, is featured on a well-known series of posters. Peter Drew Singh finds respite from the pressure of NSW politics in what sounds to me like the grimmest of situations. He’s an RFS volunteer, who enlisted after the Black Summer bushfires, but he tells me that, rather than fighting fires, most of his work has been supporting people on the worst days of their lives. Not as the boss but as the one who follows orders. “It’s not something I’ve sought to promote necessarily but plenty of people have seen me out on the fires or at car accidents and stuff, and sometimes people were a little bit surprised to see me holding a Stop/Go sign or sweeping glass off the road or rolling up a pipe or whatever it is that we’re called to do on that day. “I find it pretty rewarding. Given that I’m fairly junior in the brigade, I go there and take orders.”

Advertisement

One of the most confronting scenes he has responded to happened over Christmas while at a family dinner at a local beach. The brigade got a call and so Singh left the venue and headed two beaches over. A man had suffered a medical episode in the water and drowned. Paramedics were trying to resuscitate him. As an RFS volunteer his job wasn’t to be the hero but to help retrieve supplies from the ambulance as others worked to save the man’s life. “That’s often what you’re confronted with rather than actual fire, although we’ve had some hairy fires as well.” For the man with a title like NSW Nationals leader, his path to politics was fairly cosmopolitan. He attended UNSW and worked in a newsagent’s in Bondi. Straight out of university, Singh went to work for Qantas, in the marketing team, before working in software. He found a passion for politics after moving back home to farming. Singh has been at the scene of local tragedies as a member of the RFS. Sam Mooy While previous media reporting has painted Singh as a humble blueberry and macadamia farmer, that’s only part of the story. He was actually director of the powerful blueberry farmers co-op Oz Group in Woolgoolga, and was vice president of the Australian Blueberry Growers’ Association. The blueberry industry’s rapid expansion on the Mid North Coast hasn’t been without controversy, drawing concerns around pesticide use and lack of planning oversight. Dealing with land-use conflicts in horticulture and running the co-op was how Singh got interested in state politics. “Even liaising with our local council, who had a couple of Greens councillors, their solution was to add more regulation when they weren’t satisfied the existing regulation were being followed.

title: Living at home in your 20s used to be taboo. Now it’s a financial lifeline

MoneySavingBudgeting Living at home in your 20s used to be taboo. Now it’s a financial lifeline Nina Hendy July 28, 2026 — 11:23am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Living at home with her parents well into her 20s has resulted in a huge financial saving that has helped 25-year-old Chloe Henry get ahead in life and also helped the communications professional save for her first overseas holiday. Henry doesn’t pay any rent to her parents, instead contributing by buying some groceries and helping with the housework. Other than that, her income is hers to do with as she pleases. Communications professional Chloe Henry says she hopes to take her parents on a holiday to thank them for letting her live at home. “I’m lucky that my parents have allowed me to stay at home for as long as I want and that they’re happy to have me there. I’m off to Japan in September for my birthday, and I can’t wait,” she says. Each morning, she travels via public transport from Berwick into Melbourne, a journey that takes 90 minutes each way. But the sacrifice has been worth it, enabling her savings to quietly grow.

Advertisement

“Living at home means I’m not feeling like I’m under a price crunch. I have a savings goal in mind, and I’ve been able to reach that goal a lot faster,” she says. But the future of life on her own isn’t entirely clear. The hope is that one day, she could be in a strong enough position to be able to rent with her partner, who is still in university. “I’m pretty pessimistic about the housing market and being able to save up to move out or put a deposit on a home. A lot of my friends still live at home and don’t have plans to move out anytime soon either.” Staying put Henry is not alone. New research from AMP shows that for many, support is no longer just about the bank of mum and dad, it’s also about the house of mum and dad, with extended families open to sharing housing, costs and care in more practical ways.

Advertisement

The shift has been driven mostly by younger singles as housing affordability, rate increases and cost of living pressures combine to make living alone increasingly unaffordable. Editor's pick Opinion

Housing affordability A new type of class divide is emerging – and property is to blame Victoria Devine Money columnist The growing number of shared living arrangements is in direct response to the constant rise in living costs, which shows no sign of easing. While common in some cultures, multi-generational living isn’t the norm in Australia. But what started during the pandemic as a way to save money as housing costs bolted has now become a way of life for many. At a time when so many people are seeking financial stability, it’s understandable that living with a flatmate could be undesirable for some given that factors outside their control – such as job losses or a large unexpected bill – could impact on their ability to cover rent.

Advertisement

Generational shift Ben Hillier, general manager of retirement solutions at AMP. Natalie Boog AMP’s research found that 68 per cent of 20- to 39-year-olds support multi-generational living, but fewer than two in five people aged 65 and over do. This points to a generational shift in expectations around independence and home ownership. “As housing pressures intensify and Australia becomes increasingly multicultural, younger Australians are rethinking what the ‘Australian dream’ looks like,” explains Ben Hillier, AMP’s director of retirement. “This shift also tells us something important about confidence for retirement, which in Australia has long been tied to home ownership. Alongside super, Australians’ sense of financial security will increasingly be shaped by the household around them – how families live, what support they can provide one another and how costs and care are shared.”

Advertisement

Mortgage brokers have noticed the change in property demand too as they’re asked to help families find homes that will accommodate extended family members, says Rebecca Jarrett-Dalton of Two Red Shoes. “Our job as brokers is no longer just about securing a rate – it’s about providing creative pathways, whether it’s navigating generational wealth when buying property, or helping families explore shared ownership,” she says. As for Henry, she admits she doesn’t have all the answers about housing in the future, but does hope that one day she can thank her parents for letting her stay home well into her 20s. “Maybe I can pay for them to take a holiday one day,” she says. title: Victoria’s premier revealed after chaotic vote
text:
Ben Carroll is Victoria's new Premier after Jacinta Allan quit minutes before she was due to face a brutal leadership coup, just four months out from the state election.

Mr Carroll, who was the education minister and deputy premier, was elected unanimously by the Labor caucus on Tuesday morning after a chaotic two-hour meeting following Attorney-General and Allan supporter Sonya Kilkenny's decision to stand against Mr Carroll.

Gabrielle Williams was elected as deputy and at one stage was about to be made interim leader as caucus was deadlocked.

Advertisement Advertisement

Advertisement Advertisement

Labor managed at the last minute to avoid having an interim leader for up to six weeks ahead of the November election while the rank-and-file members of the party voted for either Mr Carroll or Ms Kilkenny.

Ben Carroll is Victoria's new Premier. Picture: NewsWire/ David Crosling

Jacinta Allan quit minutes before the expected leadership challenge. Picture: NewsWire/ David Crosling

The announcement was made just as the bells for parliament to sit rang.

"You're watching live the death of the Victorian Labor government," News24 political reporter Andrew Clennell said.

Ms Allan quit minutes before she was due to face a brutal leadership coup.

Mr Carroll had been expected to be elected without issue to take over has leader at the Labor caucus on Tuesday morning.

But the meeting descended into chaos, with Ms Kilkenny deciding to stand against Mr Carroll.

Advertisement Advertisement

Advertisement Advertisement

Media outside the closed room heard yelling, with leaks from the caucus suggesting there would be a move to install an interim leader and send the leadership vote to rank and file Labor Party members.

Mr Carroll emerged triumphant after hours of deliberation. Picture: NewsWire/ David Crosling

Clennell described the situation as "absurd".

"They've decided to burn the house down," Clennell said, as the meeting dragged on after Allan supporters pushed back on a smooth change.

Grim-faced Labor MPs walked passed journalists packing the corridor after the meeting, saying they were happy with the outcome and that it was "bad news for the Liberals".

Mr Carroll left without comment, heading straight to Government House to be sworn as Premier.

Advertisement Advertisement

Advertisement Advertisement

He is then expected to stand up for the first time as Premier on Tuesday afternoon.

New Premier's first words

In a video posted on his official social media pages, Mr Carroll said he was "honoured" to have been elected unanimously by his Labor colleagues.

"Yesterday, they asked me to put my hand up to lead our party, and I agreed. This was not an easy decision, but the stakes at this election are too high," he said.

Mr Carroll said it was time for Labor to deliver "a new direction". Picture: NewsWire/ David Crosling

"Polling says Victoria is on track for Australia's first Liberal-One Nation government - a Liberal One-Nation government that will cut school, health, and frontline services.

"Only Labor can stop the risk of a Liberal-One Nation Government that will hurt working people.

Advertisement Advertisement

Advertisement Advertisement

"It is clear that on key ssues that matter to Victorians, our government needs to go in a new direction on integrity, on community safety and on the economy.

"As Premier, I will deliver that new direction."

Mr Carroll was officially sworn in as Premier at Government House in Melbourne just before 12.50pm on Tuesday.

Allan leaves, chaos enters

Ms Allan had vowed to fight for her job, but in an address to the media at 9.30am announced she had made "the difficult decision" to stand down as premier.

Jacinta Alan has stood down as premier. Picture: NewsWire/ David Crosling

"I was prepared to put my record and my plan to a ballot of members … and I believe I would have won," Ms Allan said in announcing her resignation.

Advertisement Advertisement

Advertisement Advertisement

The Premier said her choice not to pursue the ballot of members was made because "doing so this close to an election takes up valuable resources".

"It puts the state in a position of uncertainty. That hurts the Victorian people, and I just won't do that. I am, and always have been, a team player," she said.

"I will shortly chair a caucus meeting to elect a new leader."

She said she would support Deputy Premier Ben Carroll if he put his hand up because she said she was "a team player".

"Should Ben Carroll emerge as our next Labor leader and Labor Premier, he will have my congratulations and unqualified support by making this decision, because it is the right thing by the Labor Party and by the Victorian people."

Ms Allan said her mother taught her 'to never give up'. Picture: NewsWire / Josie Hayden

Ms Allan, who is not expected to stand for her seat of Bendigo East in November, said she would have "relished" taking on the Coalition in the state election.

Advertisement Advertisement

Advertisement Advertisement

"I fight for working class families, it's in my blood and I would have absolutely relished the fight this November," she said.

"I was more than ready.

"I saw off two Liberal leaders, now, I expect my successor will see off the third.

"And if they don't, One Nation certainly will."

Just weeks ago, Mr Carroll promised Ms Allan he wouldn't be asking her to step aside, but that all changed this week when he flagged he would challenge the Premier.

Jacinta Allan defended her record as Premier as she resigned at a press conference on Tuesday. Picture: NewsWire/ David Crosling

Allan defends record

During her resignation speech, Ms Allan listed several of her government's achievements, including falling crime rates and budget recalibration.

Advertisement Advertisement

Advertisement Advertisement

"I leave immensely proud. I inherited a toughened crime rate … crime is now falling for the first time since Covid. I inherited a budget deficit … my team and I made savings, the budget today is now in surplus," she said.

"We not only made public transport free during a fuel crisis, we made public transport free for kids forever."

Ms Alan said her government had built 121 new schools and 12 new hospitals, and she was "goddamn proud" of the Melbourne Metro.

"They are not just projects, they are assets that will improve our lives," she said.

Ms Alan defended her record. Picture: NewsWire/ David Crosling

A government that 'listened to girls'

In a moment of emotional tenderness, Ms Allan said she was proud to have led "a government that listened to girls about their health".

Advertisement Advertisement

Advertisement Advertisement

"I'm a woman, I'm a mum, I've lived with endometriosis, and I almost lost my daughter at birth. These experiences not only defined who I am, they defined what my government should do for working women," she said.

"I lead a government that listened to girls about their health. Tens of thousands of you wrote in, and we opened 15 women's health clinics across the state. You can get the pill at the chemist without having to pay to see a GP.

"If your child is sick in the middle of the night, you can visit Australia's first virtual emergency department … this is what happens when women are heard."

How the challenge unfolded

On Monday morning, a delegation of MPs and key factional leaders within the Victorian Labor caucus entered Ms Allan's office and demanded her resignation under threat of a leadership spill.

Deputy Premier Ben Carroll is poised to take over. Picture: NewsWire / Josie Hayden

Among the delegation were several members of Ms Allan's ministerial cabinet, including Police Minister Anthony Carbines Public Transport Minister Gabrielle Williams and Mental Health Minister Ingrid Stitt.

Advertisement Advertisement

Advertisement Advertisement

Ms Allan reportedly demanded the resignation of each minister who entered the room.

Despite pressure from major party figures, Ms Allan still has vocal supporters, including Ms Kilkenny, who said Ms Allan had her "full support" on Sunday.

Shortly after the meeting took place, Mr Carroll was approached by members of the caucus and told he would receive the majority of support in a leadership spill if he nominated himself against his boss.

On the day of Ms Allan's appointment as premier, Mr Carroll said he 'couldn't think of a better job in the world' than to serve her. Picture: NewsWire / David Crosling

Carroll supported Allan just weeks ago

Mr Carroll, who once said he "couldn't think of a better job in the world than to support Jacinta", released a statement later on Monday, saying the decision to topple his former boss hadn't been easy.

"This decision is not easy, but the stakes at the upcoming election are simply too high," Mr Carroll said.

"The prospect of a Liberal-One Nation government that will cut school, health and frontline services is simply too high a risk to ignore."

The last year of Ms Allan's stint as premier has been characterised by consistent month-on-month polling decline and controversies surrounding alleged corruption within state infrastructure projects, highly publicised violent crime and a public school system crumbling under the weight of repeated pay disputes with teaching unions.
